1.title: A machine that makes new things
body:
Where we meet the machines, and find out what this whole book is trying to explain.

Start with a story

Riya is in Class 10. One evening she types this into a chatbot: "Write a four-line poem about my grandmother's mango pickle." Three seconds later, a poem appears. It rhymes. It mentions the sun-dried mangoes and the big glass jar.

Riya is puzzled. She hadn’t seen that poem before. So where did it come from? The machine made it.

That is the question this book answers: how can a machine make something new?

1.1 Two kinds of smart machines

Think of two students in an art class.

  • The judge. You show her a painting and she says, "This is a cat" or "This is a dog". She recognises things.
  • The artist. You give him a blank page and he paints a new cat that nobody has seen before.

Both are clever, but the artist's job is harder. To judge, you only need to notice a few clues such as whiskers and pointed ears. To paint, you must know everything about how a cat looks: the fur, the eyes, the shadow under the chin.

Machines that judge are called discriminative models. Machines that create are called generative models. "Generate" simply means "produce". This book is about the artists.

1.2 Generative machines you already know

TypeYou give itIt gives backFamous examples
Text generatorA question or instruction in wordsNew text: an answer, a story, even computer codeChatGPT, Gemini, Claude
Image generatorA description, like "a tiger riding a bicycle"A new picture that matchesDALL·E, Stable Diffusion
Speech generatorA written sentenceA sound file of a voice saying itText-to-speech tools

The thing you type in is called a prompt.

1.3 A new word: "conditional"

Notice that none of these machines produce just anything. The poem had to be about mango pickle, because Riya asked for that. The output depends on a condition, and the condition is the prompt.

So scientists call ChatGPT a conditional text generator, and DALL·E a conditional image generator. "Conditional" only means "the request guides what the model tries to produce".

Common confusion

"The machine has stored millions of poems and pictures, and it just searches for the right one." No. A search engine finds things that already exist. A generative model creates an output from patterns it has learned. Sometimes it can repeat material it has seen. How that is possible is exactly what the coming chapters build up to.

1.4 The road ahead

The course this book follows covers six families of generative machines. "Deep generative models" (DGMs for short) is the formal name for all of them. The word deep is there because each one has a deep neural network inside, which you will meet in Chapter 5.

#FamilyShort nameOne-line idea
1Generative Adversarial NetworksGANsTwo networks play a game against each other: a forger and a detective
2Variational Auto-EncodersVAEsSqueeze data into a small code, then rebuild it
3Diffusion modelsDDPMsStart from pure noise and clean it step by step into a picture
4Auto-regressive modelsAR / LLMsPredict the next word, again and again (this is how ChatGPT writes)
5State-space modelsSSMsA newer alternative to family 4 (examples: S4, Mamba)
6Alignment methodsPPO, DPOTeaching a language model to behave the way people prefer

This book (Parts 1 to 4) covers the foundation and then family 1, the GANs. GANs are no longer the best tool for most jobs, so why start there? Because they teach the core principles of generative modelling very clearly. Once you understand GANs, the other families become much easier.

Two promises from the course that this book keeps:

  • It is mathematical. We will not just say "the machine learns". We will write down exactly what it does. Do not worry: every piece of maths is taught from the beginning.
  • It does not depend on the type of data. The same ideas work for pictures, text and sound. We will mostly use pictures as examples because they are easy to imagine.

Try it

For each machine, say whether it is a judge (discriminative) or an artist (generative): (a) an app that tells you which bird is in your photo, (b) an app that turns your sentence into a song, (c) the spam filter in your email.

Show answer

(a) Judge. It only labels the photo. (b) Artist. It produces a new song. (c) Judge. It only decides "spam" or "not spam".

Chapter 1 recap

  • A generative model is a machine that produces new data: text, images, speech.
  • A discriminative model only recognises or labels data.
  • Conditional means the output must match a prompt.
  • We will study the maths behind these machines, starting with GANs.

2.title: Everything is a list of numbers
body:
A computer cannot see a cat. It can only see numbers. So first we learn how a picture becomes numbers.

The problem

We want to do maths on pictures and poems. But maths works on numbers, and a photo of a cat is not a number. Before anything else, we need a way to write any piece of data as numbers.

2.1 Describing a student with numbers

Suppose your school keeps three facts about each student: height in cm, weight in kg, and maths marks.

StudentHeightWeightMarksWritten as a list
Aman1605278(160, 52, 78)
Bhavna1524591(152, 45, 91)
Chetan1716466(171, 64, 66)

Each student has become an ordered list of 3 numbers. Such a list is called a vector. The count of numbers in the list is called the dimension. Here the dimension is 3.

You already know this idea from coordinate geometry. A point on a graph is (x, y): a list of 2 numbers, so it lives in 2 dimensions. Aman is a point in 3 dimensions. We cannot draw 10 or 1000 dimensions, but the idea is the same: a longer list. Nothing mysterious.

2.2 A picture is also a list

Zoom into any photo on your phone and you will see tiny squares. Each square is a pixel. In a black-and-white photo, every pixel stores one number for its brightness: 0 means black, 255 means white, and numbers in between are shades of grey.

A colour photo needs three numbers per pixel: how much Red, how much Green and how much Blue. Mixing these three makes every colour your screen can show. These three layers are called channels.

2.3 How big is the list for a real photo?

Take a small colour photo with 400 rows and 400 columns of pixels. Let us count, one step at a time.

StepCalculationResult
Pixels in the photo400 rows × 400 columns1,60,000
Numbers per pixelRed, Green, Blue3
Total numbers1,60,000 × 34,80,000

So one small photo is a single point in a space of 4,80,000 dimensions. Aman needed 3 numbers. A photo needs nearly five lakh. This is why people say that this subject deals with high-dimensional data.

2.4 The notation scientists use

Now we can read the first line of maths from the lectures. It looks scary, but you already know every piece of it.

D = { x1, x2, … , xn }    and    xi ∈ ℝd
SymbolRead it asMeaning
D"the dataset"The whole collection of examples we have, such as an album of photos
x1, x2"x one, x two"The first photo, the second photo. Each is a full list of numbers
n"n"How many examples there are (how many photos)
xi"x i"Any one of them, "photo number i"
ℝ"the real numbers"All ordinary numbers: 3, −7.2, 0.5 and so on
ℝd"R d"All possible lists made of d real numbers
∈"belongs to"You met this in sets
d"d"The dimension: how many numbers are in each list

So the whole line just says: "We have n examples, and each example is a list of d numbers."

Example. Aman's list (160, 52, 78) is made of three real numbers, so we can write (160, 52, 78) ∈ ℝ3. A 400 × 400 colour photo is a list of 4,80,000 real numbers, so it belongs to ℝ4,80,000.

Common confusion: n and d

Students mix these up all the time. n counts examples. d counts numbers inside one example. An album of 1000 photos, each 400 × 400 in colour, has n = 1000 and d = 4,80,000.

Text and sound also become lists of numbers. For sound, the numbers are the height of the sound wave measured thousands of times every second. For text, each word piece gets its own numbers. The details differ, but the principle never changes: data = points in a high-dimensional space.

Try it

1. A black-and-white photo has 28 rows and 28 columns. What is d?
2. You have 60,000 such photos. What is n?
3. A colour photo is 100 × 200 pixels. What is d?

Show answer

1. 28 × 28 × 1 = 784.   2. n = 60,000.   3. 100 × 200 × 3 = 60,000. (Notice that 60,000 appears as n in one question and as d in another. They are different things.)

Chapter 2 recap

  • A vector is an ordered list of numbers. Its length is the dimension, d.
  • A picture is a vector: one number per pixel, times 3 for colour.
  • A 400 × 400 colour photo has d = 4,80,000.
  • A dataset D has n examples, each a point in ℝd.

3.title: Chance has a shape
body:
The lecturer said the whole course looks at these machines through probability, the maths of chance. So we begin with a single dice.

The problem

If you ask an image generator for "a cat" twice, you get two different cats. There is luck involved. To talk about luck properly, we need the language of probability. You learnt a little of it in Class 10. Here we add four new ideas: random variable, distribution, density and sampling.

3.1 Quick revision

The probability of something is a number from 0 to 1 that tells you how often it happens. 0 means never, 1 means always. For a fair dice, each face comes up one time in six, so the probability of a 4 is 1/6, which is about 0.167.

3.2 Random variable: a number decided by luck

Before you roll the dice, you do not know the result. Call the unknown result X. This X is a random variable: a quantity whose value is decided by chance.

After you roll, you get an actual value, say 4. That 4 is called a sample (or an instance, or a draw) of X. Roll again and you get another sample.

Common confusion

The random variable is the dice still in your hand, full of possibilities. The sample is the number showing after it lands. One random variable can give you as many samples as you like.

3.3 Distribution: the full table of chances

A probability distribution is the complete list of every value the random variable can take, along with the probability of each. Here are two different dice.

Face123456Total
Fair dice1/61/61/61/61/61/61
Cheater's dice0.050.050.100.100.200.501

Both dice show the same six faces. What makes them different is the distribution. The cheater's dice lands on 6 half the time. Two rules always hold: every probability is between 0 and 1, and all of them add up to exactly 1.

Now the phrase in this chapter's title. Draw a bar for each face, with height equal to its probability. The fair dice gives six equal bars: a flat shape. The cheater's dice gives a staircase rising to the right. A distribution has a shape. When scientists say "two distributions are different", picture two different bar charts.

3.4 A more interesting shape: two dice

Roll two fair dice and add them. The total can be anything from 2 to 12, but not with equal chance. There are 36 possible pairs. Only one pair gives 2 (that is 1+1), but six pairs give 7 (1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1).

Total23456789101112
Pairs12345654321
Probability1/362/363/364/365/366/365/364/363/362/361/36

The shape is a hill: low at the ends, highest in the middle. Remember this hill. We meet its famous cousin in Section 3.6.

3.5 When the values are not whole numbers: density

A dice has only six outcomes. But what about the height of a student? It could be 156.2 cm, or 156.23 cm, or 156.2317 cm. There are endlessly many possible values. We cannot make a table with endless columns.

So we use the trick you learnt in the statistics chapter: group the values into classes and draw a histogram. Here are the heights of 100 students.

Height (cm)140–145145–150150–155155–160160–165165–170170–175
Students41224302082
Fraction0.040.120.240.300.200.080.02

Now imagine measuring a lakh of students and making the classes only 1 mm wide. The bars become so thin that their tops join into a smooth curve. That smooth curve is called the probability density function, or just the density.

How do you read a density curve?

  • Where the curve is high, values are common. Where it is low, values are rare.
  • The probability of landing between two values equals the area under the curve between them. In the table above, the chance of a height between 150 and 160 is 0.24 + 0.30 = 0.54.
  • The total area under the whole curve is 1, just as the fractions in the table add to 1.

Common confusion: density is not probability

The height of the curve at one exact point is not a probability. The chance that a student is exactly 156.231700000… cm is practically zero. Only areas are probabilities. Think of the curve's height as "how crowded it is around here".

In the lectures, the true distribution of the data is written with a fancy ℙx and its density with a plain px. The lecturer himself says he will use the two words as if they meant the same thing, and so will we. For this book, think of both as "the shape of the chances".

3.6 The most famous shape: the bell curve

The hill from the two-dice table, and the hill of student heights, are close to a shape that appears everywhere in nature: marks in an exam, weights of mangoes, errors in measurements. It is called the normal distribution or Gaussian distribution (after the mathematician Gauss), or simply the bell curve.

A bell curve is fully described by just two numbers:

  • The mean: where the centre of the bell sits. You know the mean as the average.
  • The variance: how wide the bell is. Small variance means a thin, tall bell (values huddle near the mean). Large variance means a wide, flat bell (values are scattered). The square root of the variance is called the standard deviation, and it is measured in the same units as the data.

Example of variance. Variance is the average of the squared distances from the mean. Take two groups of three test scores, both with mean 5.

ScoresMeanDistances from the meanSquaredVariance (average of the squares)Standard deviation
4, 5, 65−1, 0, 11, 0, 12 ÷ 3 = 0.67√0.67 = 0.82
1, 5, 95−4, 0, 416, 0, 1632 ÷ 3 = 10.67√10.67 = 3.27

Same centre, very different spread. The first group huddles near 5 (thin bell). The second is scattered (wide bell).

The short way to write it is N(mean, variance). The simplest one has mean 0 and variance 1. It is written N(0, 1) and called the standard normal. If you take samples from it, about 68 out of 100 fall between −1 and 1, about 95 out of 100 fall between −2 and 2, and almost none go beyond ±3.

The symbol ~ means "is drawn from". So z ~ N(0, 1) is read "z is a sample drawn from the standard bell curve".

What about lists of numbers? In the lectures you will see z ~ N(0, I) with z ∈ ℝk. This simply means: make a list of k numbers, where each number is drawn separately from the standard bell curve. The I is a tidy way of saying "each has variance 1 and they do not influence one another". For k = 4, one sample might be (0.31, −1.20, 0.05, 0.87). A random variable whose value is a whole list like this is called a vector-valued random variable.

3.7 Sampling

Sampling means getting actual values out of a distribution. Rolling a dice is sampling. A helpful picture: write numbers on a huge pile of chits, where common values are written on many chits and rare values on few. Put them in a bag, shake, and pull one out. That is one sample.

Computers are very good at sampling from simple distributions such as N(0, 1). One line of code gives you as many as you want. Keep this fact in your pocket. It becomes the key to Chapter 6.

Try it

1. Using the cheater's dice table, what is the probability of getting 5 or 6?
2. Using the two-dice table, what is the probability that the total is 10 or more?
3. Which bell is wider: N(0, 1) or N(0, 9)?
4. True or false: "The density at 156 cm is 0.3, so 30% of students are exactly 156 cm."

Show answer

1. 0.20 + 0.50 = 0.70.   2. (3 + 2 + 1)/36 = 6/36 = 1/6.   3. N(0, 9), because its variance is larger. Its standard deviation is √9 = 3.   4. False. Only areas under the curve are probabilities.

Chapter 3 recap

  • Random variable: a quantity decided by chance. Sample: one actual outcome of it.
  • Distribution: the complete description of the chances. It has a shape.
  • For continuous values the shape is a smooth curve called the density. Areas are probabilities, and the total area is 1.
  • N(0, 1) is the standard bell curve. N(0, I) is a list of such numbers.
  • ~ means "is drawn from". Computers can sample from N(0, I) easily.

4.title: The secret rulebook
body:
Now we put Chapters 2 and 3 together and state, precisely, the problem that every generative model is trying to solve.

A thought experiment

Take a 400 × 400 colour image. It is a list of 4,80,000 numbers. Fill every one of those numbers by rolling a dice. What picture do you get?

You get the "snow" of a television with no signal. Do it a crore times and you will still get snow, never a cat. Yet somewhere among all the possible lists of 4,80,000 numbers are every cat photo ever taken, and every cat photo that could ever be taken. They are just extremely rare among all the possibilities.

So there must be some hidden rule that says: "this list of numbers looks like a real photo, and that one is rubbish." We call this hidden rule the secret rulebook.

4.1 The rulebook is a distribution

In Chapter 3 a distribution told us which dice faces are common and which are rare. The secret rulebook does the same job for images. It gives a high density to lists of numbers that look like real photos, and a density of nearly zero to snow.

This rulebook is written ℙx, or px when we mean its density. It is called the true data distribution.

The most important fact about it: nobody knows it. No human can write a formula that takes 4,80,000 numbers and tells you how cat-like they are. It is unknown.

4.2 What we do have: samples

We do not have the rulebook, but we have something produced by it: real photos. Every real cat photo in our album is a sample drawn from ℙx, just as each roll is a sample from the dice.

It is like this. You are not allowed to examine the cheater's dice. But you are given a notebook with 1000 of its past rolls. From the notebook you can already guess a lot about the dice, such as "6 comes up very often".

Now you can read the next line from the lectures:

D = { x1, x2, … , xn }  ~  iid  ℙx  (unknown)

In words: "Our dataset is n samples drawn from an unknown distribution ℙx." Only one new word is left: iid.

4.3 What does "iid" mean?

It stands for independent and identically distributed. It is two promises about how the data was collected.

PromiseMeaningDice examplePhoto example
IndependentKnowing one sample tells you nothing about anotherThe dice does not remember its last rollPhoto 1 and photo 10 were taken separately, at different times and places
Identically distributedEvery sample comes from the same rulebookYou used the same dice every timeAll photos come from the one distribution ℙx

In symbols the lectures write xi ⫫ xj, where ⫫ means "is independent of".

Common confusion: independent photos, not independent pixels

The lecturer stops to stress this, so we will too. Independence is between one photo and another photo. It is not between the numbers inside one photo.

Inside a photo, pixels depend on each other heavily. If one pixel is sky-blue, its neighbour is almost surely sky-blue too. That dependence between pixels is what makes a picture a picture and not snow. We never assume pixels are independent.

Why assume a single rulebook? For mathematical ease. Guessing one unknown distribution is hard enough. Guessing many at once would be far harder. And one rulebook can be very broad. For ChatGPT-style models, the dataset is a gigantic collection of documents from the internet, and ℙx is the one distribution that covers all of it: recipes, cricket reports, physics notes, everything.

4.4 The problem, stated properly

The generative modelling problem

Given: n samples x1, …, xn drawn iid from an unknown distribution ℙx.

Goal: (1) estimate ℙx, and (2) learn to sample from it.

"Estimate" means make a good guess of the rulebook. "Learn to sample" means be able to pull out brand-new chits from the same bag. A new sample from the cat rulebook is a new cat photo.

This also answers Riya's question from Chapter 1. The new samples are not copies of photos in the dataset. If you learn the cheater's dice well and build your own, your dice will produce fresh rolls with the same pattern, not a replay of the notebook. In the same way, a generative model produces new data that follows the same rulebook as the old data.

One note for later. Some models write down their guess of the rulebook clearly. That is called explicit estimation. Other models never write it down at all, but can still produce samples from it. That is called implicit estimation. GANs, which fill most of this book, are the implicit kind. Almost every generative model, of either kind, learns to sample.

4.5 Judge versus artist, in this new language

Back to the two students of Chapter 1. A discriminative model (the judge) learns something written p(y | x). The bar "|" is read "given". So this is "the probability of label y, given the photo x", for example "given this photo, the chance it is a cat is 0.93". The judge can label photos but does not learn to produce them.

A generative model (the artist) goes after the distribution of the data itself, and its main job is to sample from it.

Try it

1. You photograph the same cat 500 times in one minute, without moving the camera. Is this dataset a good iid sample of "all cat photos"? Why?
2. In your own words, why can't the model just memorise the dataset and show those photos again?

Show answer

1. No. The photos are nearly the same, so they are not independent, and they describe one cat in one pose instead of the full variety of cats.   2. Because the goal is to sample from the rulebook ℙx, which contains endlessly many possible photos. The dataset is only a few samples from it. Repeating them would be searching, not generating.

Chapter 4 recap

  • Real data follows a hidden distribution ℙx, the "secret rulebook". It is unknown.
  • Our dataset is n iid samples from it: independent of each other, all from the same rulebook.
  • Independence is across examples, never across pixels.
  • Goal: estimate ℙx and learn to sample from it.

5.title: The three-step recipe
body:
Every generative model in the course, from GANs to ChatGPT, follows the same three steps. Learn the recipe once and you have a map for everything else.

A tiny version of the problem

Your friend has a bent coin and will not tell you how bent it is. That hidden truth is the rulebook. You are given a record of its tosses. Your job is to build your own coin that behaves the same way.

We will solve this tiny problem with the same three steps that the big machines use. To keep the first pass simple, we will pretend for a moment that we can peek at the truth: the coin lands heads with probability 0.7. In Section 5.5 we take the peeking away.

5.1 Step 1: build a guess with knobs

We do not know the true coin. So we build a model coin with one adjustable setting: its probability of heads. Call that setting θ (the Greek letter theta).

  • Set θ = 0.5: a fair coin.
  • Set θ = 0.9: a coin that almost always lands heads.

Each value of θ gives a different distribution. Together they make a whole family of distributions, one for each knob setting. An adjustable setting like this is called a parameter, so this is a parametric family. We write the model's distribution as pθ, read "p theta": the distribution you get when the knob is at θ.

You have seen parameters before. In the line y = mx + c, the numbers m and c are parameters. Change them and you get a different line from the family of all straight lines.

Detour: what is a neural network?

A coin needs one knob. An image rulebook needs far more. For that, scientists use a neural network. We will open one up properly later. For now, this picture is enough.

A neural network is a function: a machine that takes numbers in and gives numbers out, like y = mx + c but far bigger. Inside it are many simple calculations stacked in layers. Each calculation has its own knobs, and a large network may have crores of them. When there are many layers, the network is called deep. That is where "deep" in "deep generative models" comes from.

Why this particular machine? Because of a remarkable property called universal approximation: with enough knobs, a neural network can imitate practically any function as closely as you like. It is like clay. A straight line can only ever be a straight line, but clay can be pressed into any shape.

From now on, θ stands for all the knobs of the network together: not one number, but a giant list of them.

In the lectures, the word model means exactly this: the adjustable guess pθ, represented by a deep neural network.

5.2 Step 2: measure how far the guess is from the truth

We need a single number that says how different two distributions are. Such a number is called a divergence. Think of it as a distance between two shapes of chance.

For the coin, a simple choice is the gap between the two heads-probabilities:

D = | 0.7 − θ |

The bars mean absolute value, which you know from Class 9 and 10: drop the minus sign, so |−0.2| = 0.2.

Whichever divergence we use, it must behave like a sensible distance. Two properties are always demanded:

  1. It is never negative: D ≥ 0.
  2. It is zero only when the two distributions are exactly the same. The lectures write "D = 0 iff px = pθ". The word iff is short for "if and only if". It means the statement works in both directions: same distributions give zero, and zero means same distributions.

The standard way to write a divergence is with a double bar between the two distributions:

D( px ‖ pθ )

Read it as "the divergence between the true distribution and the model's distribution". The double bar is only a separator, like a comma.

Our coin gap is the baby version. Real divergences for complicated distributions have names like KL and JS. They get a full chapter of their own (Chapter 8).

5.3 Step 3: turn the knob until the distance is smallest

Now try different knob settings and compute the distance for each.

Knob θ0.10.30.50.60.70.80.9
Working|0.7−0.1||0.7−0.3||0.7−0.5||0.7−0.6||0.7−0.7||0.7−0.8||0.7−0.9|
Distance D0.60.40.20.100.10.2

The smallest distance is 0, and it happens at θ = 0.7. Hunting for the best setting like this is called optimisation. Finding the smallest value is called minimisation.

Detour: min and argmin

Two different questions can be asked about the table above.

  • "What is the smallest distance?" The answer is 0. This is the min.
  • "Which knob setting gives the smallest distance?" The answer is 0.7. This is the argmin, short for "the argument that minimises".

An everyday version: in a race, min is the winning time (say 11.2 seconds) and argmin is the name of the winner. We care about argmin, because we want to know where to set the knobs.

The best setting is marked with a star: θ*, read "theta star". We can now read one of the most important lines in the whole course:

θ* = argminθ  D( px ‖ pθ )

In plain words: "θ* is the knob setting that makes the model's distribution as close as possible to the true distribution."

Because D can never go below 0, and it reaches 0 only when the two distributions match, driving D down to its minimum pulls pθ towards px. Once they match, our model coin behaves like the secret coin, and the problem is solved.

5.4 The recipe in the lecturer's words

  1. Assume a parametric family on px, written pθ, represented by a deep neural network. This is the model.
  2. Define and estimate a divergence (distance) between pθ and px.
  3. Solve an optimisation problem over the parameters θ to minimise that divergence.

The lecturer adds that this is not a sacred law. It is a pattern he noticed by looking across all the generative models, and it is a very useful map.

5.5 Wait. Did we cheat?

Yes, and you should object. In Step 2 we used the true value 0.7. But the whole point is that the truth is unknown. With a real dataset, we cannot compute D( px ‖ pθ ) by peeking at px, because we do not have px. We only have samples from it.

The lecturer raises this objection himself. He asks whether we are assuming the very thing we set out to find. He calls it a very valid question, and the rest of Part 1 exists to answer it. The answer is one of the cleverest ideas in the subject: a divergence can be worked out from samples alone, with no formula for either distribution. Hold on to this question. Chapters 7 to 10 answer it.

Try it

A secret dice shows 6 with probability 0.4. Your model dice shows 6 with probability θ, and you use D = |0.4 − θ|.
1. Find D for θ = 0.1, 0.25, 0.4 and 0.5.
2. What is the min? What is the argmin?
3. Can D ever be −0.1?

Show answer

1. 0.3, 0.15, 0 and 0.1.   2. min = 0, argmin = 0.4, so θ* = 0.4.   3. No. A divergence is never negative.

Chapter 5 recap

  • Step 1: choose a model pθ, a guess with knobs θ. In practice it is a deep neural network.
  • Step 2: choose a divergence D( px ‖ pθ ). It is ≥ 0, and equals 0 iff the two distributions are the same.
  • Step 3: find θ* = argminθ D( px ‖ pθ ).
  • min is the smallest value. argmin is the setting that achieves it.
  • Open question: how do we measure D when px is unknown?

6.title: The sampling machine
body:
The recipe gives us a good guess of the rulebook. But the goal had two parts, and the second was to produce new samples. This chapter shows the trick that does it.

The problem

Suppose a magician hands you the perfect rulebook for cat photos. Give it any list of 4,80,000 numbers and it tells you how cat-like the list is. Can you now produce a cat photo?

Not easily. You would have to test lists one at a time, and nearly every list is snow. A rulebook that scores pictures is not a machine that makes pictures. We need another idea.

6.1 The key trick: reshape easy randomness

Here is a fact from probability that the lecturer uses: if you pass a random variable through a function, the output is also a random variable, and it has a different distribution. Which distribution it has depends on the function.

Let us see this with a fair dice. Call its result z. Every face has probability 1/6.

Function A: g(z) = z² (square the result).

Roll z123456
Output z²149162536
Probability1/61/61/61/61/61/6

The outputs are now 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and 36. That is a different distribution from the original dice: the values are spread out differently.

Function B: g(z) = "Heads if z ≤ 4, otherwise Tails".

Roll z123456
OutputHHHHTT

Four of the six faces give Heads, so P(Heads) = 4/6 ≈ 0.67. We have turned a dice into a bent coin. The dice supplied the randomness. The function gave it a new shape.

Notice that the function itself contains no luck at all. Give it the same input and it always returns the same output. Such a function is called deterministic. All the randomness comes from z.

6.2 Add a knob, and you have a tiny generative model

Put a knob inside function B: gθ(z) = "Heads if z ≤ θ, otherwise Tails".

Knob θ12345
Faces giving Heads11, 21, 2, 31, 2, 3, 41 to 5
P(Heads) of the output1/6 ≈ 0.172/6 ≈ 0.333/6 = 0.504/6 ≈ 0.675/6 ≈ 0.83
Distance from a secret coin with P(Heads) = 0.670.500.330.1700.17

Suppose the secret coin lands heads two times in three. The last row shows that the best knob is θ* = 4. With that setting, here is how you make a new sample of the secret coin: roll the dice, pass the result through gθ*, and read the output. Each roll gives a fresh coin toss with the right chances.

Look at what happened. We never wrote down a formula for the coin's distribution. We built a machine whose outputs follow that distribution. This is the whole idea of a generative model, in miniature.

6.3 The real thing

Now make three replacements and you have the setup used in the lectures.

Toy versionReal versionSymbol
A dice rollA list of k numbers, each drawn from the standard bell curve. Its distribution is simple and known, so sampling is easy (Section 3.7)z ~ N(0, I), z ∈ ℝk
A rule with one knobA deep neural network with a huge number of knobs. It takes k numbers in and gives d numbers outgθ
A coin tossA list of d numbers, which is an imagex̂ = gθ(z)

The little cap on x̂ is read "x hat". The hat means "made by our model", to keep it apart from a real data point x. The starting randomness z is often called noise.

The lecturer says z has "some arbitrary but known distribution". Arbitrary means we are free to choose it. Known means we must choose one we can sample from. The standard bell curve is the usual choice.

Because z is random and gθ is a deterministic function, the output x̂ is a random variable with its own distribution. That distribution depends on the knobs θ. This is our model distribution from Chapter 5, pθ. So every output of the network is a sample from pθ.

6.4 Joining the machine to the recipe

At the start, the knobs are set randomly, so the network turns noise into rubbish. Its distribution pθ is far from the truth px. Now apply Step 3 of the recipe and find the best knobs:

θ* = argminθ  D( px ‖ pθ )

Once this is solved, pθ* is close to px. Then two things are true together:

  1. We have estimated the rulebook, implicitly. We hold no formula for it. But the network's outputs follow it, so in a real sense the network contains it.
  2. We can sample from it. Draw a fresh z from N(0, I), pass it through gθ*, and out comes a sample from pθ*, which is close to px. In effect we are sampling from the secret rulebook.

Both goals from Chapter 4 are met. And since each new z gives a new output, the machine can produce endless new samples. As the lecturer points out, these outputs are not members of the dataset. We are sampling from the underlying distribution, not replaying what is already there.

Common confusion

"The network receives a real photo and edits it." No. When generating, the network receives only noise z. The real photos were used earlier, to decide where the knobs should be set. That earlier stage is called training.

6.5 Four questions that the rest of the course answers

The plan is clear, but four big questions are still open. The lecturer ends by listing them and says that each different way of answering them gives a different kind of generative model.

#QuestionWhere we answer it
1How can we compute a divergence without knowing px or pθ?Chapters 7 to 10
2Which divergence should we choose?Chapter 8, and again in Part 4
3How should we design the network gθ, and so pθ?Part 3
4How do we actually solve the minimisation?Part 2

Try it

1. With a fair dice z and the rule "Heads if z is even, otherwise Tails", what is P(Heads)?
2. Design a rule that turns a fair dice into a coin with P(Heads) = 1/3.
3. In the real setup, which of these is random and which is deterministic: z, gθ, x̂?
4. A network takes k = 100 noise numbers and outputs a 400 × 400 colour image. How many numbers come out?

Show answer

1. Faces 2, 4 and 6 give Heads, so 3/6 = 0.5.   2. One answer: "Heads if z ≤ 2". Any rule that picks exactly two faces works.   3. z is random. gθ is deterministic. x̂ is random, because its input is random.   4. d = 4,80,000.

Chapter 6 recap

  • Passing a random variable through a function gives a new random variable with a new distribution.
  • The generator gθ is a neural network that turns noise z ~ N(0, I) into a sample x̂ = gθ(z).
  • The outputs follow a distribution pθ that depends on the knobs.
  • Choose θ* = argminθ D( px ‖ pθ ). Then the machine samples from something close to the real rulebook.
  • Four questions remain: how to compute D, which D, which network, and how to minimise.
Coming next: Chapters 7 to 10. We answer the first big question. How do you measure the distance between two distributions when you have never seen either of them, and hold only samples? On the way we learn logarithms, the Σ sign, area under a curve, averages, and a beautiful idea called the law of large numbers.

7.title: A small toolkit of maths
body:
Six tools, each one small. We need all six in the next three chapters, so we collect them first.

7.1 Tool 1: the Σ sign (adding many things)

You will need this for: the batch averages of Chapter 13, and almost every formula from here on.

Writing "add up all these numbers" again and again is tiring. Mathematicians use the Greek capital letter sigma, Σ, as a short form for "sum".

Σi=14 ai  =  a1 + a2 + a3 + a4

Read it as "the sum of ai, for i going from 1 to 4". If the four numbers are 5, 2, 7 and 6, the sum is 20. The average of n numbers is then written very compactly:

average = 1n Σi=1n ai

For our four numbers this is 20 ÷ 4 = 5.

7.2 Tool 2: expectation (the long-run average)

You will need this for: the final result of Part 1 and the GAN objective. Both are made of expectations.

Take the cheater's dice from Chapter 3. If you rolled it a huge number of times and averaged all the results, what number would you get? There is a way to know without rolling at all: multiply each value by its probability and add.

Face x123456Sum
Probability p(x)0.050.050.100.100.200.501
x × p(x)0.050.100.300.401.003.004.85

The long-run average is 4.85. This number is called the expectation or expected value, written with a special letter 𝔼:

𝔼[X] = Σ x · p(x) = 4.85

Why does this work? In 100 rolls you expect about 50 sixes, 20 fives, and so on. Add them all up and divide by 100, and you get exactly the calculation in the table.

Common confusion

"Expected value" does not mean "the value you expect to see". The dice can never show 4.85. It is the average over many rolls.

Expectation of a function. Suppose you win h(x) = x² rupees when the dice shows x. Your long-run average winning uses the same idea: multiply each prize by its probability and add.

Face x123456Sum
Prize h(x) = x²149162536
Probability0.050.050.100.100.200.501
h(x) × p(x)0.050.200.901.605.0018.0025.75
𝔼p[h(x)] = Σ h(x) · p(x) = 25.75

The small p under the 𝔼 tells you which distribution the luck comes from. With a fair dice the same prize rule would give 91 ÷ 6 ≈ 15.17. Same function, different distribution, different expectation. Keep an eye on that little subscript in the coming chapters.

7.3 Tool 3: the ∫ sign (Σ for smooth curves)

You will need this for: reading the definition of the f-divergence in Chapter 8.

For a dice we added over six values. For something continuous, like height, there are endlessly many values. Go back to the height table of Chapter 3 and compute the average height using the middle of each class, exactly as you did in Class 10 statistics.

Class middle x142.5147.5152.5157.5162.5167.5172.5Sum
Fraction of students0.040.120.240.300.200.080.021
x × fraction5.7017.7036.6047.2532.5013.403.45156.6

Each fraction is the area of one bar in the histogram: the bar's height (the density) times its width. If we make the bars thinner and thinner, the sum has more and more terms, each one tiny. In the limit of endlessly thin bars, the sum gets a new symbol:

𝔼[h(x)] = ∫ h(x) p(x) dx

How to read each piece:

  • ∫ is a stretched letter S, for "sum". It is called the integral sign.
  • p(x) is the height of the density curve at x.
  • dx is the width of one endlessly thin bar. So p(x) dx is the area of that bar, which is the probability of landing in it.
  • h(x) is the value we are averaging.

So an integral is nothing more than a sum over endlessly many thin slices. You do not need to know how to calculate integrals for this book. You only need to read them: whenever you see ∫ (something) p(x) dx, say to yourself "the average of that something, when x is drawn from p". The lecturer mentions that this rule has a funny name: the law of the unconscious statistician.

A small ∫ with a set written below it, such as ∫𝒳, means "add over all possible values of x". The set 𝒳 is called the support: the region where the distributions live. For images it is ℝd.

7.4 Tool 4: logarithms

You will need this for: the KL divergence in Chapter 8 and the GAN objective in Chapter 12.

A logarithm answers one question: "how many times must I multiply?" Since 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, we say "log of 8 to the base 2 is 3". The log turns the big number 8 into the small count 3.

In this subject people use a special base called e, a fixed number about equal to 2.718. The log with base e is called the natural logarithm, written ln or simply log. You do not have to compute it by hand. A calculator does that. You only need its behaviour:

u0.10.250.512410
log u−2.303−1.386−0.69300.6931.3862.303

Four facts to remember, all visible in the table:

  1. log 1 = 0.
  2. Numbers bigger than 1 have a positive log. Numbers between 0 and 1 have a negative log.
  3. log(a × b) = log a + log b. Check: log 4 = log(2 × 2) = 0.693 + 0.693 = 1.386.
  4. log(a ÷ b) = log a − log b. Check: log 0.5 = log(1 ÷ 2) = 0 − 0.693.

The log is only defined for positive numbers. The reverse of the log is written et ("e to the power t"): since log 2 = 0.693, we have e0.693 = 2.

Why do logs show up everywhere in this subject? Because of fact 1 and fact 2 together. If two probabilities are equal, their ratio is 1 and the log is 0. If they differ, the log moves away from 0. The log of a ratio is a natural "how different are these two?" meter.

7.5 Tool 5: convex functions (bowls)

You will need this for: the rule for which penalty functions are allowed (Chapter 8) and the mirror trick of Chapter 10.

Draw the graph of f(u) = u². It looks like a bowl. A function whose graph is bowl-shaped is called convex.

Here is the precise test. Pick any two points on the graph and join them with a straight line (a chord). If the chord never dips below the curve, the function is convex.

With numbers: the points are u1 = 1 (height 1) and u2 = 3 (height 9). Halfway between them is u = 2.

  • Height of the chord at the halfway point: the average of the two heights, (1 + 9) ÷ 2 = 5.
  • Height of the curve at the halfway point: 2² = 4.

5 ≥ 4, so the chord is above the curve. In words: "the average of the heights is at least the height at the average". The lectures write this test with two weights α1 and α2 (alpha one, alpha two) that are each between 0 and 1 and add up to 1:

α1 f(u1) + α2 f(u2)  ≥  f( α1u1 + α2u2 )

We used α1 = α2 = ½, the halfway point. Other weights test other points along the chord. The same rule keeps working with many points and many weights: for a convex function, a weighted average of heights ≥ the height at the weighted average. We will use this fact once, in Chapter 8, and it will do something lovely.

Example with unequal weights. Take α1 = 0.25 and α2 = 0.75 with the same two points. Left side: 0.25 × 1 + 0.75 × 9 = 7. Right side: the weighted average of the inputs is 0.25 × 1 + 0.75 × 3 = 2.5, and 2.5² = 6.25. Since 7 ≥ 6.25, the test passes again.

Example of a function that fails. Take f(u) = −u², an upside-down bowl. At u = 1 and u = 3 the heights are −1 and −9. The chord at the halfway point is (−1 − 9) ÷ 2 = −5. The curve at the halfway point is −(2²) = −4. Is −5 ≥ −4? No. The chord is below the curve, so this function is not convex.

7.6 Tool 6: max and sup

You will need this for: Chapter 10, and the min–max game of Part 2.

max means the largest value. The max of {3, 9, 5} is 9. In the lectures you will see the word sup (short for supremum). For this book, read "sup" as "max". The lecturer says the same thing. (The difference only matters in rare cases where the largest value is approached but never actually reached.)

Written with a variable underneath, supt { … } means "try every possible t and keep the biggest result". It is the opposite twin of the min from Chapter 5.

Example. Find supt { 6t − t² }. Try some values:

t12345
6t − t²58985

The biggest result is 9, so the sup is 9. It is reached at t = 3.

Try it

1. Compute Σi=13 i².
2. A coin gives ₹10 for heads (probability 0.7) and ₹0 for tails. What is the expected winning?
3. Without a calculator, find log 8 using log 2 = 0.693.
4. Is log 0.9 positive or negative?
5. Is f(u) = u² convex by the chord test with u1 = 0 and u2 = 4, at the halfway point?

Show answer

1. 1 + 4 + 9 = 14.   2. 10 × 0.7 + 0 × 0.3 = ₹7.   3. log 8 = log(2 × 2 × 2) = 3 × 0.693 = 2.079.   4. Negative, since 0.9 is below 1.   5. Chord height (0 + 16)/2 = 8. Curve height at u = 2 is 4. Since 8 ≥ 4, it passes.

Chapter 7 recap

  • Σ means add. ∫ means add over endlessly many thin slices.
  • Expectation 𝔼p[h(x)] is the long-run average of h when x is drawn from p. It equals Σ h(x)p(x), or ∫ h(x)p(x)dx.
  • log 1 = 0. Logs of ratios measure how different two numbers are.
  • Convex = bowl-shaped: average of heights ≥ height at the average.
  • sup ≈ max: the largest value.

8.title: Measuring the distance between two distributions
body:
In Chapter 5 we used a baby distance for coins. Now we meet the real thing: a whole family of distances called f-divergences.

The problem

Two shopkeepers each sell three flavours of ice cream. We want one number that says how differently their customers behave. For a coin, comparing one probability was enough. For three flavours, or for images, we need a general method.

8.1 The idea: compare point by point, using ratios

To keep the arithmetic small we go back to coins. Let the true coin be px and the model coin be pθ.

OutcomeTrue pxModel pθRatio u = px ÷ pθ
Heads0.70.51.4
Tails0.30.50.6

For each outcome we take the ratio of the two probabilities and call it u. If the two coins were identical, every ratio would be exactly 1. Here the ratios are 1.4 and 0.6, so the model gives heads too little weight and tails too much.

Now a three-line plan for turning ratios into one number:

  1. Choose a penalty function f(u) that says how bad a ratio u is. A ratio of 1 is perfect, so we demand f(1) = 0.
  2. Compute the penalty at every outcome.
  3. Take the average of the penalties, with the model's probabilities pθ as weights.

That is the whole definition. For outcomes you can count:

Df( px ‖ pθ ) = Σx  pθ(x) · f( px(x)pθ(x) )

For continuous data such as images, the Σ becomes ∫ (Tool 3). This is the form written in the lectures:

Df( px ‖ pθ ) = ∫𝒳 pθ(x) · f( px(x)pθ(x) ) dx

This is called the f-divergence. The small f in Df reminds us that the answer depends on which penalty function we picked.

A worry you might have: x is a list of 4,80,000 numbers, so how can we put it inside f? We do not. A density takes the whole list and returns one non-negative number ("how crowded it is here"). The ratio of two such numbers is one positive number, and that single number is what goes into f. This is why f only needs to accept positive numbers. The lectures write this as f : ℝ+ → ℝ, "f takes a positive real number and returns a real number".

8.2 What kind of f is allowed?

RequirementWhy
f(1) = 0No penalty where the two distributions agree
f is convex (a bowl, Tool 5)This is what makes the divergence never negative. See 8.3
f is "left semi-continuous"A technical condition that rules out badly behaved jumps in the graph. Every f we use is smooth enough, so you can safely set this aside

The letter u inside f(u) is a dummy variable, a placeholder. f(u) = u² and f(t) = t² are the same function.

8.3 Two properties, and why the first one is true

Chapter 5 said any sensible divergence needs two properties. The f-divergence has both, for any allowed f:

  1. Df ≥ 0 always.
  2. Df( px ‖ pθ ) = 0 iff px = pθ.

First reading? You may skip the next four lines

What follows is the reason behind property 1. If it feels heavy, accept the two properties, jump to Section 8.4, and come back later. Nothing ahead depends on having followed the reason.

Here is why property 1 holds. It takes four lines and uses only Tool 5.

Df = Σ pθ · f(u) a weighted average of heights of f, with weights pθ
     ≥ f( Σ pθ · u ) convex: average of heights ≥ height at the average
     = f( Σ pθ · pxpθ ) = f( Σ px ) pθ cancels
     = f(1) = 0 probabilities add to 1, and f(1) = 0

So Df ≥ 0. The two requirements on f (convex, and zero at 1) are exactly the two things this argument used. Check the weighted average of the ratios with our coins: 0.5 × 1.4 + 0.5 × 0.6 = 1. It always comes out as 1. And check the conclusion with f(u) = u log u: the weighted average of the heights is 0.5 × f(1.4) + 0.5 × f(0.6) = 0.5 × 0.471 + 0.5 × (−0.306) = 0.082, which is indeed ≥ f(1) = 0.

Property 2 has an easy half: if the distributions are equal, every ratio is 1, every penalty is f(1) = 0, and the total is 0. The other half (zero happens only then) is true for the penalty functions used in this book.

8.4 Example 1: KL divergence

Choose f(u) = u log u. First check the requirement: f(1) = 1 × log 1 = 1 × 0 = 0. Good. Now put u = px / pθ into the definition.

Df = ∫ pθ(x) · f( px(x)pθ(x) ) dx the definition
     = ∫ pθ(x) · [ px(x)pθ(x) · log px(x)pθ(x) ] dx f(u) = u log u
     = ∫ px(x) · log px(x)pθ(x) dx pθ outside cancels pθ below

This is the famous Kullback–Leibler divergence, or KL divergence, written DKL( px ‖ pθ ). In words: the average, over the true distribution, of the log of the ratio. The log-ratio meter of Tool 4, averaged.

With our coins:

Outcomepxpθratiolog(ratio)px × log(ratio)
Heads0.70.51.40.3360.2355
Tails0.30.50.6−0.511−0.1532
DKL( px ‖ pθ )0.0823

Notice that one row is negative, yet the total is positive, exactly as property 1 promised.

A surprise: KL is not symmetric. Swap the two coins and recompute.

Outcomepθpxratio pθ/pxlog(ratio)pθ × log(ratio)
Heads0.50.70.714−0.336−0.1682
Tails0.50.31.6670.5110.2554
DKL( pθ ‖ px )0.0872

0.0823 is not 0.0872. The distance from A to B differs from the distance from B to A.

DKL( px ‖ pθ ) ≠ DKL( pθ ‖ px )

The first is called the forward KL, the second the reverse KL.

Common confusion: a divergence is not a ruler

The distance from your home to school equals the distance from school to home. A divergence does not have to obey that. This is why the word is "divergence" and not "distance", and why the order around the double bar ‖ matters. All a divergence promises is: never negative, and zero only for identical distributions.

8.5 Example 2: JS divergence

If the lack of symmetry bothers you, choose a different penalty:

f(u) = ½ [ u log u − (u + 1) log( u + 12 ) ]

Check: f(1) = ½ [ 0 − 2 × log 1 ] = 0. Good. The divergence this gives is the Jensen–Shannon divergence, or JS divergence. Compute it for the coins using the definition directly:

Outcomepθratio uf(u)pθ × f(u)
Heads0.51.40.016740.00837
Tails0.50.60.025270.01263
DJS0.0210

Working for the heads row, with log 1.4 = 0.3365 and log 1.2 = 0.1823: f(1.4) = ½ [ 1.4 × 0.3365 − 2.4 × 0.1823 ] = ½ [ 0.4711 − 0.4376 ] = 0.0167. (The 1.2 comes from (u + 1) ÷ 2 = 2.4 ÷ 2.)

Swap the two coins and you get 0.0210 again. JS is symmetric. There is a friendlier way to think about it. Make a "midpoint" coin m that averages the two: heads 0.6, tails 0.4. Then JS is the average of two KLs, each measured to that midpoint: ½ KL(px ‖ m) + ½ KL(pθ ‖ m) = ½ (0.0216) + ½ (0.0204) = 0.0210. Same number.

Remember JS. The lecturer says a version of it is what the famous GAN uses, and we will see exactly how in Part 2.

8.6 Example 3: total variation distance

Choose f(u) = ½ |u − 1|. Check: f(1) = ½ × 0 = 0. Substituting, the pθ cancels once more and leaves ½ Σ |px − pθ|: half the total of the absolute gaps.

For the coins: ½ ( |0.7 − 0.5| + |0.3 − 0.5| ) = ½ (0.2 + 0.2) = 0.2.

Look at that. It equals |0.7 − 0.5|, which is the baby distance we invented in Chapter 5. Our simple coin gap was the total variation (TV) distance all along.

8.7 Why have a whole family?

Penalty f(u)DivergenceOur coinsSymmetric?
u log uKL0.0823No
½ [ u log u − (u+1) log((u+1)/2) ]JS0.0210Yes
½ |u − 1|Total variation0.2Yes

Each choice of f gives a divergence with its own character, and so a generative model with its own behaviour. Having a family lets us pick the one whose properties suit the job. The good news: the method we build in Chapters 9 and 10 works for any f in the family, all at once.

Try it

True coin: heads 0.8, tails 0.2. Model coin: heads 0.5, tails 0.5.
1. Find the two ratios u.
2. Find the total variation distance.
3. Find the forward KL. (You need log 1.6 = 0.470 and log 0.4 = −0.916.)
4. If the model becomes heads 0.8, tails 0.2, what are all three divergences?

Show answer

1. 0.8/0.5 = 1.6 and 0.2/0.5 = 0.4.   2. ½ (0.3 + 0.3) = 0.3.   3. 0.8 × 0.470 + 0.2 × (−0.916) = 0.376 − 0.183 = 0.193.   4. All zero, because the distributions are now identical.

Chapter 8 recap

  • An f-divergence averages a penalty f of the ratio px/pθ, weighted by pθ.
  • f must be convex with f(1) = 0. That guarantees Df ≥ 0, with 0 iff the distributions match.
  • u log u gives KL (not symmetric: forward and reverse differ).
  • Two other choices give JS (symmetric, used by GANs) and total variation.

9.title: Averages instead of formulas
body:
We have a fine definition of distance. We just cannot compute it. This chapter finds the escape route.

The problem, in full

Look at the f-divergence formula again. To use it we need the value of px(x) and of pθ(x) at every possible x. But:

  • We do not know px. It is the secret rulebook.
  • We do not know pθ either. The generator hands us samples, not a formula for its density.
  • Even if we knew both, the ∫ runs over a space of 4,80,000 dimensions. Adding up slices in that many directions is practically impossible for any computer.

The lecturer calls this the most important challenge in building generative models, and says it appears across all of machine learning: we must optimise things that involve distributions without having the distributions.

9.1 What we do have

DistributionDo we have its formula?Do we have samples?
True pxNoYes. The dataset D is exactly that
Model pθNoYes, as many as we want. Draw a z, compute gθ(z), repeat

So the new goal, in the lecturer's words: an algorithm that minimises Df between px and pθ without knowing either of them, but having samples from both.

9.2 The key idea: an average of samples can replace an integral

Remember the cheater's dice. In Section 7.2 we computed its expectation from the probability table: 𝔼[X] = 4.85. That needed the table, which is the "formula".

Now suppose the table is hidden. You may only roll the dice and write down what you see. Can you still find 4.85? Just average your rolls. Here is what happened in one computer experiment:

Number of rolls n101001,00010,0001,00,000True value
Average of the rolls4.104.744.7544.8594.8464.85
Average of (roll)²20.124.6824.9425.8125.7125.75

With 10 rolls the average is poor. With a lakh of rolls it is almost exact. And we never looked at the probability table. This is one of the oldest and most useful results in statistics.

The law of large numbers

If x1, x2, …, xn are drawn iid from px, then for large n:

1n Σi=1n h(xi)  ≈  𝔼px[h(x)]  =  ∫ h(x) px(x) dx

The left side needs only samples. The right side needs the formula. They are (nearly) equal.

The lectures write "Lt n → ∞" in front, read "in the limit as n goes to infinity". It means the approximation gets better and better as n grows, and becomes exact in the limit. The symbol ≈ means "approximately equal". This also shows why the iid assumption of Chapter 4 matters: the law is stated for iid samples.

Common confusion: the samples must come from the right distribution

The lecturer stresses this. Averaging rolls of a fair dice will never give you the expectation of the cheater's dice. The samples you average must be drawn from the very distribution that appears in the expectation. This is why the little subscript under 𝔼 matters so much.

9.3 So are we done? Not yet

The law says: any quantity of the form "average of h(x) under px" can be estimated from samples. So if we could write the f-divergence as expectations with respect to px and pθ, we could compute it from samples and then optimise it.

Is the f-divergence already in that form? Compare:

What we can estimateWhat the f-divergence looks like
Formula∫ h(x) · p(x) dx∫ f( px(x) / pθ(x) ) · pθ(x) dx
What goes inside the functionthe sample x itself. We have ita ratio of two unknown densities. We do not have it

It looks similar: a density times a function. But in our law, the function h must be something we can evaluate on a sample. Here the "function" needs the densities themselves, which are the very things we lack. The unknown densities are trapped inside f.

So the remaining job is clear. As the lecturer puts it, we must somehow pull px and pθ out of the function f, so that what is left are plain expectations. That needs one more tool, and it is the subject of Chapter 10.

Try it

1. You toss a coin 10 times and get 7 heads. Winning ₹10 per head, what is your sample-average winning per toss? What does the law of large numbers say this estimates?
2. You want 𝔼pθ[h(x)]. Which samples should you average over: the dataset, or outputs of the generator?
3. Why can we not just average f( px(x) / pθ(x) ) over generator outputs?

Show answer

1. (7 × 10 + 3 × 0) ÷ 10 = ₹7. It estimates the expected winning per toss, 10 × P(heads).   2. Outputs of the generator, since those are the samples of pθ.   3. Because to compute that value for even one sample we would need the numbers px(x) and pθ(x), and we know neither.

Chapter 9 recap

  • We cannot compute Df directly: both densities are unknown and the integral is over a huge space.
  • We do have samples from both: the dataset, and generator outputs.
  • Law of large numbers: the average of h over samples ≈ the expectation of h.
  • Plan: rewrite Df using only expectations over px and pθ.
  • Obstacle: the densities are stuck inside f.

10.title: The mirror function and the lower bound
body:
The last and cleverest step of Part 1. We free the densities from inside f, and a second neural network quietly enters the story.

The plan for this chapter

Every convex function has a partner, called its conjugate. The partner lets us rewrite f(u) in a form where u appears only as a plain multiplier, no longer locked inside. Once u = px/pθ is a plain multiplier, it cancels against the pθ in front, and expectations appear. The lecturer warns that this part is slow and fussy, and asks you to bear with him. We will take it in six small steps.

10.1 The conjugate of a convex function

If f(u) is convex, its conjugate function f*(t) (read "f star of t") is defined like this:

f*(t) = supu { u t − f(u) }

In words: "for a given number t, try every u, compute u × t − f(u), and keep the biggest result." The letter t is another dummy variable.

Notice what kind of definition this is. To get one value of f* you must solve a small maximisation problem. The lecturer calls it a pointwise definition: one optimisation per point.

Worked example. Take f(u) = u² and find f*(2). We need the largest value of 2u − u².

u00.511.52

The biggest value is 1, reached at u = 1. So f*(2) = 1. Repeat for other values of t:

The pattern is f*(t) = t²/4. (You can confirm it by completing the square: ut − u² = t²/4 − (u − t/2)², which is largest when the bracket is zero.) So the conjugate of the bowl u² is another bowl, t²/4.

What it means in a picture. ut is a straight line through the origin with slope t. So ut − f(u) is the gap between that line and the curve, and f*(t) is the largest gap. The lecturer describes the same thing from the other side: the conjugate builds straight lines that sit below the curve, and keeps the tightest one.

10.2 Two properties of the conjugate

  1. f* is also convex. (Our t²/4 is a bowl.)
  2. The conjugate of the conjugate is the original function. Like a mirror image of a mirror image:
f(u) = supt { t u − f*(t) }

Check property 2 with our example at u = 3, where we should recover f(3) = 9. We need the largest value of 3t − t²/4:

guess t246810
3t612182430
t²/41491625

The largest value is 9, exactly f(3). The mirror works.

The fact that everything rests on

Read the table once more. Every guess of t gave a number that is ≤ 9. Only the best guess reached 9. So:

  • For any t:   t u − f*(t) ≤ f(u). A wrong guess still gives a valid lower bound.
  • For the best t: equality.

And look at the shape of t u − f*(t). The variable u is no longer locked inside a function. It is just multiplied by t. That is the escape we were looking for.

10.3 The derivation, in six steps

First reading? Here is the short version

The six steps below are the hardest page of the book. If you get lost, read only this: "we replace f by its mirror form, the best guess t becomes a function T(x), and after cancelling we are left with two averages." Then go to Section 10.4, where every step is repeated with plain numbers, and come back here afterwards.

Step 1. Start from the definition and name the ratio u.

Df( px ‖ pθ ) = ∫ pθ(x) · f(u) dx,    where u = px(x)pθ(x)

Step 2. Replace f(u) by its mirror form from property 2.

Df = ∫ pθ(x) · supt { t u − f*(t) } dx

Step 3. Put the ratio back in place of u.

Df = ∫ pθ(x) · supt { t · px(x)pθ(x) − f*(t) } dx

Step 4. The best t is different at every x, so t becomes a function T(x). This is the subtle step. The "sup" sits inside the integral, so at each point x there is a separate little maximisation, and its answer depends on the ratio at that x. One best t for this image, another best t for that image.

A rule that gives one number for each x is simply a function of x. Call it T(x). Instead of solving endlessly many small problems (one t per x), we can solve one big problem: search for the best function T.

Df = supT ∫ pθ(x) · { T(x) · px(x)pθ(x) − f*( T(x) ) } dx

An everyday picture: to get the highest total marks for a class, each student needs the study plan that suits them. "Find the best plan for every student" is the same as "find the best rule that assigns a plan to each student".

Step 5. Admit that our search may not be perfect: "=" becomes "≥". In practice we cannot search over every imaginable function. We search inside some collection of functions, written 𝒯 (for example, everything a particular neural network can represent). The lectures write T(x) ∈ 𝒯, and note that each such T takes an x and returns a number that f* can accept (in symbols, T : 𝒳 → dom f*).

The collection 𝒯 may not contain the perfect function T*. If it does not, the best we find inside 𝒯 gives something smaller than the true value. Because of the key fact from 10.2 (any guess gives a lower bound), it can never be larger. So we write:

Df ≥ supT ∈ 𝒯 ∫ pθ(x) · { T(x) · px(x)pθ(x) − f*( T(x) ) } dx

Step 6. Multiply out the bracket. In the first term, the pθ in front cancels the pθ underneath. This is the moment the trapped densities walk free.

Df ≥ supT [ ∫ px(x) · T(x) dx  −  ∫ pθ(x) · f*( T(x) ) dx ]

Now read each integral with Tool 3: "a function of x, times a density, added up" is an expectation.

The result of Part 1

Df( px ‖ pθ )  ≥  supT [ 𝔼px[ T(x) ] − 𝔼pθ[ f*( T(x) ) ] ]

10.4 The same six steps again, with numbers

Symbols are easier to believe when you see them at work. Take our two coins (true: heads 0.7, tails 0.3; model: heads 0.5, tails 0.5) and the KL penalty f(u) = u log u. From Chapter 8 we know the answer we must reach: 0.0823.

We need the conjugate of this f. It is f*(t) = et−1. Do not just accept that. Check it at t = 1, where the formula gives e0 = 1. The definition says: find the largest value of u × 1 − u log u.

The largest is 1. The formula is right at this point.

Step 1 with numbers. The ratios are u = 1.4 for heads and 0.6 for tails. With a calculator, f(1.4) = 1.4 × log 1.4 = 0.4711 and f(0.6) = 0.6 × log 0.6 = −0.3065.

Df = 0.5 × 0.4711 + 0.5 × (−0.3065) = 0.2355 − 0.1532 = 0.0823

Steps 2 and 3 with numbers. Replace each f(u) by "the largest value of t u − et−1". That is one small search for heads and another for tails.

Heads (u = 1.4): guess t11.21.3361.5

For heads the best guess is t = 1.336, and it gives 0.4711, which is exactly f(1.4). For tails the best guess is t = 0.489, and it gives −0.3065, exactly f(0.6). The mirror form reproduces f.

Step 4 with numbers. Notice that the best t was different for the two outcomes: 1.336 for heads, 0.489 for tails. A rule that says "for heads use 1.336, for tails use 0.489" is a function of the outcome. That is all T(x) is:

T(heads) = 1.336,    T(tails) = 0.489

For a coin, "searching over all functions T" just means "searching over all pairs of numbers". For images it means one number for every possible image, which is why we will need a neural network to hold it.

Step 5 with numbers. Suppose our search is limited: we are only allowed functions that give the same number c to heads and tails. The best such function turns out to be c = 1, and its value is 0.7 × 1 + 0.3 × 1 − (0.5 × e0 + 0.5 × e0) = 1 − 1 = 0. That is below the true 0.0823. A limited collection 𝒯 that does not contain the best function gives a smaller number. This is why "=" had to become "≥".

Step 6 with numbers. Use the best T and split the sum into its two averages.

𝔼px[ T ]: average of T under the true coin0.7 × 1.336 + 0.3 × 0.4891.0823

We have reached 0.0823 again, and look at how: the last table never used a ratio of probabilities. It only needed averages, one under each coin. Averages are what samples can give us.

10.5 Why this is such good news

Look at the right-hand side. There is no density formula anywhere. There are two averages:

TermMeaningHow to estimate it (law of large numbers)
𝔼px[ T(x) ]Average of T over real dataApply T to the photos in the dataset and average
𝔼pθ[ f*(T(x)) ]Average of f*(T) over generated dataApply T, then f*, to outputs of the generator and average

Both need only samples, and samples are exactly what we have. The first big question from Chapter 6 ("how can we compute a divergence without knowing px or pθ?") is answered.

The price we paid: we do not get Df itself. We get a lower bound on it, a number guaranteed to be no bigger than the true divergence. The better our search for T, the closer the bound climbs to the true value. Think of measuring the height of a ceiling by jumping: every jump shows the ceiling is at least that high, and your best jump gives your best estimate.

Searching over functions (instead of over numbers) is called a variational method. So this result is known as the variational lower bound on the f-divergence, and using it to train generators is variational divergence minimisation.

10.6 Checking the bound with other guesses

Do not just trust the algebra. Take our coins and the KL divergence, which we know equals 0.0823. For f(u) = u log u, the conjugate is f*(t) = et−1, as checked in Section 10.4. For a coin, a "function T" is just two numbers: one for heads and one for tails. Try three different choices.

Every choice gives a number that is at most 0.0823. The lazy guess gives 0, a true but useless bound. A better T gives 0.0741. The best T reaches 0.0823, the exact KL divergence. Just as the ceiling picture said.

Look also at what the best T does: it gives a higher score to heads, the outcome the true coin produces more often than the model does, and a lower score to tails. In a sense T has learnt to tell where the real data and the model disagree. Hold on to that thought.

10.7 What comes next

We now have two things that need to be found:

  • the function T, which we want to push up (sup), to make the bound as close to the true divergence as possible, and
  • the generator's knobs θ, which we want to use to push the divergence down (argmin).

One side pushes up while the other pushes down. Does that sound like two players in a game? It is. Represent T with a second neural network and you have, almost exactly, a Generative Adversarial Network. That is where Part 2 begins.

Try it

1. For f(u) = u², find f*(4) by filling a table of 4u − u² for u = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
2. Using f*(t) = t²/4, compute t u − f*(t) at u = 2 for t = 2, 4 and 6. Which is largest, and what does it equal?
3. Someone finds a function T that gives a bound of 0.05. What can they say about the true divergence?
4. In the final result, which term is averaged over the dataset and which over generator outputs?

Show answer

1. Values: 0, 3, 4, 3, 0. The largest is 4, so f*(4) = 4, which matches 4²/4.   2. t = 2: 4 − 1 = 3. t = 4: 8 − 4 = 4. t = 6: 12 − 9 = 3. The largest is 4 = 2² = f(2).   3. Only that it is at least 0.05. It could be larger.   4. 𝔼px[T(x)] uses the dataset. 𝔼pθ[f*(T(x))] uses generator outputs.

Chapter 10 recap, and the end of Part 1

  • Every convex f has a conjugate f*(t) = supu { ut − f(u) }, and f(u) = supt { tu − f*(t) }.
  • Any t gives a lower bound on f(u). The best t gives equality.
  • Using this inside Df, the best t at each x becomes a function T(x), and the densities cancel out.
  • Result: Df ≥ supT [ 𝔼px T(x) − 𝔼pθ f*(T(x)) ]. Both terms can be estimated from samples.
  • The whole of Part 1 in one sentence: we want a machine whose outputs follow the data's hidden distribution, we measure the gap with an f-divergence, and we can estimate that gap from samples alone by training a helper function T.
Coming next: Part 2, Chapters 11 to 14. The helper function T becomes a second neural network, the two networks start competing, and the Generative Adversarial Network is born.

11.title: From one network to two
body:
The helper function T gets a body of its own, and we discover that our two networks want opposite things.

The problem

We have a generator gθ and a goal: θ* = argminθ Df( px ‖ pθ ). We cannot compute Df. But we have a lower bound on it that we can compute. How do we turn that into a recipe a computer can follow?

11.1 Minimise the bound instead

We cannot minimise the true divergence, so we do the next best thing and minimise its lower bound:

θ* = argminθ Df( px ‖ pθ ) what we really want
     ≈ argminθ [ lower bound on Df ] what we can actually do
     = argminθ [ maxT ( 𝔼px[ T(x) ] − 𝔼pθ[ f*(T(x)) ] ) ]

Notice the honest "≈" on the second line. The bound is not the divergence. It is close to it only when the search for T is done well. So there are two searches, one inside the other:

  • The inner one, max over T, runs over a class of functions 𝒯. Its job is to make the bound tight, so that it is a faithful measure of the divergence.
  • The outer one, min over θ, runs over the knobs of the generator. Its job is to make that measured divergence small.

11.2 Give T a body: a second neural network

How do we search over functions? Chapter 5 told us: a neural network is clay that can take the shape of almost any function. So we represent T by a second neural network. Its knobs get a new name, w, so they do not get mixed up with the generator's knobs θ. We write the network as Tw(x).

Searching over functions T now becomes searching over knob settings w. With this, the objective becomes:

θ*, w* = argminθ maxw [ 𝔼px[ Tw(x) ] − 𝔼pθ[ f*( Tw(x) ) ] ]

The quantity in the square brackets depends on both sets of knobs, so it gets a name, J(θ, w):

J(θ, w) = 𝔼px[ Tw(x) ] − 𝔼pθ[ f*( Tw(x) ) ]     and     θ*, w* = argminθ maxw J(θ, w)

Where is θ hiding in J? In the second term. The subscript pθ says that the x there is a generated sample, gθ(z).

NetworkKnobsTakes inGives outName
gθθnoise za generated sample x̂Generator, because it samples from the distribution we care about
Twwa sample x (real or generated)one number, a scoreCritic or discriminator

Detour: a quick look inside a neural network

We have called a network "a function with knobs". Here is a little more, enough for the words used in the lectures.

The basic unit is a neuron. It does two things. First it takes a weighted sum of its inputs: multiply each input by a knob (called a weight), add them, and add one more knob (called a bias). Then it passes the result through a simple fixed function called an activation.

Example: inputs (2, 1), weights (0.5, −1), bias 0.5.

  • Weighted sum: 2 × 0.5 + 1 × (−1) + 0.5 = 0.5.
  • Activation: a common one says "keep the number if it is positive, otherwise output 0". Here the output stays 0.5.

Many neurons side by side form a layer. The outputs of one layer become the inputs of the next. Stack many layers and you have a deep network. All the weights and biases together are the knobs.

Three terms you will meet:

  • MLP (multi-layer perceptron) or FNN (feed-forward network): the plain kind, where every neuron of one layer connects to every neuron of the next.
  • CNN (convolutional neural network): a kind designed for images. Part 3 explains it.
  • Linear layer: a layer that does only the weighted sum, with no activation. Its output can be any real number, positive or negative, large or small.

11.3 A tug of war

Look again at argminθ maxw J(θ, w). The same quantity J is pulled in two opposite directions:

  • the critic's knobs w are tuned to make J as large as possible, and
  • the generator's knobs θ are tuned to make J as small as possible.

A problem with a "min" and a "max" over the same objective is called a saddle point optimisation problem. Why "saddle"? Think of a horse's saddle, or a pass between two mountains. Stand at the centre. Walk forward or backward along the horse and the surface goes up. Walk sideways and the surface goes down. That centre is a saddle point.

A tiny example with one knob each (real networks have crores, but the lecturer uses single numbers for the picture too): let J(θ, w) = θ² − w².

J = θ² − w²w = −2w = −1w = 0w = 1w = 2
θ = −203430
θ = −1−3010−3
θ = 0−4−10−1−4
θ = 1−3010−3
θ = 203430

Look at the centre cell, θ = 0, w = 0, where J = 0. Move up or down the middle column (change θ): the value rises to 1 and 4. Move left or right along the middle row (change w): the value falls to −1 and −4. The w player, who wants a large J, cannot do better than w = 0. The θ player, who wants a small J, cannot do better than θ = 0. Neither can improve by moving alone. That balance point is what we are seeking.

Since each network tries to undo what the other is doing, the lecturer says they can be seen as adversaries, which means opponents. Saddle point problems are therefore also called adversarial problems. Now you know where the "A" in GAN comes from: Generative Adversarial Networks.

Common confusion: the critic is not the enemy

The two networks compete, but the critic is doing the generator a service. Its job is to measure how far the generated data is from the real data. A weak critic gives a loose bound, which is a blunt measuring tape. The generator needs a sharp one to improve.

11.4 One practical detail: the critic's last layer

In Chapter 10 we noted that T must return numbers that f* can accept. The set of numbers a function accepts is called its domain, written dom f*. In symbols, Tw : 𝒳 → dom f*.

This matters because some functions cannot accept every number. You know that √ cannot take a negative number, and log cannot take zero or a negative number. Depending on which f we chose, f* may accept only a limited range.

A neural network ending in a linear layer can output any real number. So, in practice, the critic is built in two parts:

Tw(x) = σf( Vw(x) )
PartWhat it isIn symbols
Vw(x)The main network, ending in a linear layer. Takes a sample, returns any real numberVw : 𝒳 → ℝ
σf(v)A fixed final activation (σ is the Greek letter sigma) that squeezes any real number into the range f* accepts. It has no knobs. It is chosen to suit the particular f, so it is called an f-divergence-specific activationσf : ℝ → dom f*

Putting this into J gives the general form that works for any f-divergence:

J(θ, w) = 𝔼px[ σf( Vw(x) ) ] − 𝔼pθ[ f*( σf( Vw(x) ) ) ]

Try it

1. In argminθ maxw J(θ, w), which network wants J large and which wants it small?
2. For J = θ² − w², the players are at θ = 1, w = 2. What is J? If only the w player may move, where should it go?
3. A neuron has inputs (1, 3), weights (2, −1) and bias 0. What is its weighted sum?
4. Why can the critic not simply end in a linear layer for every choice of f?

Show answer

1. The critic (w) wants it large. The generator (θ) wants it small.   2. J = 1 − 4 = −3. The w player should move to w = 0, where J = 1, the largest value in that row.   3. 1 × 2 + 3 × (−1) + 0 = −1.   4. Because a linear layer can output any real number, but f* may accept only some numbers. The activation σf fixes this.

Chapter 11 recap

  • We minimise the lower bound in place of the true divergence.
  • T is represented by a second network Tw, the critic / discriminator.
  • The objective is θ*, w* = argminθ maxw J(θ, w): a saddle point, or adversarial, problem.
  • The critic is Tw(x) = σf( Vw(x) ): a network plus an activation chosen for the particular f.

12.title: The forger and the detective
body:
Everything so far worked for any f-divergence. Now we fix one particular f, do a little algebra, and the famous GAN appears.

A story to hold on to

A forger prints fake ₹500 notes. A detective at the bank checks every note and says "real" or "fake".

At first the forger is hopeless and the detective catches every fake. But each time a note is caught, the forger learns what gave it away and fixes that flaw. The detective, seeing better fakes, learns to look for finer details. Round after round, both improve.

Where does it end? When the fakes are so good that the detective can only guess, like tossing a coin. At that point the forger is making notes that cannot be told apart from real ones.

The forger is the generator. The detective is the discriminator. "Discriminate" here simply means "tell apart". This chapter shows that the story is not just a nice picture. It drops straight out of the maths of Part 1.

12.1 The GAN's choice of f

For the GAN, the penalty function is:

f(u) = u log u − (u + 1) log(u + 1)

The lecturer notes that this is "similar to" the JS divergence of Chapter 8 "but not quite exactly". Let us see precisely how. Check the value at 1:

f(1) = 1 × log 1 − 2 × log 2 = 0 − 2 × 0.693 = −1.386

It is not 0. So this f does not quite follow the rule f(1) = 0. What it produces is the JS divergence, doubled, with a constant subtracted:

Df = 2 × DJS − log 4      (log 4 = 1.386)

Check with our coins from Chapter 8, where DJS = 0.0210. Computing Σ pθ f(u) directly with this f gives −1.3443. And 2 × 0.0210 − 1.3863 = −1.3443. They match.

Does the constant spoil anything? No. Subtracting the same number from every value does not change where the smallest value is. (If every student loses 5 marks, the ranking stays the same.) The divergence is still smallest exactly when px = pθ. The only change is that the smallest value is now −log 4 = −1.386 and not 0. Remember this number. It returns in Chapter 13.

12.2 The two ingredients that go with this f

The recipe of Chapter 11 needs the conjugate f* and the activation σf. For this f they are as follows (the lecture states them, and so do we):

IngredientFormulaNote
Conjugatef*(t) = −log( 1 − et )The log needs 1 − et to be positive. That happens only when t is negative. So dom f* = ℝ−, the negative numbers
Activationσf(v) = −log( 1 + e−v )1 + e−v is always bigger than 1, so its log is positive, so σf is always negative. Just what f* needs

As before, do not just accept the conjugate. Check it at one point. Take t = log 0.5 = −0.693. The formula gives f*(t) = −log(1 − 0.5) = −log 0.5 = 0.693. The definition says: find the largest value of u t − f(u).

u0.512
f(u) = u log u − (u+1) log(u+1)−0.955−1.386−1.910
