The largest is 0.693, the same as the formula. And a quick check of the activation: σf(0) = −log(1 + e0) = −log 2 = −0.693, a negative number, as promised.

Detour: the sigmoid function

One function appears in almost every neural network book:

sigmoid(v) = 11 + e−v
v−4−2−10124
sigmoid(v)0.0180.1190.2690.50.7310.8810.982

It takes any real number and squeezes it into the range between 0 and 1. Very negative inputs go near 0, very positive inputs go near 1, and 0 goes to exactly 0.5. Its graph is a smooth S, which is where the name comes from.

A number between 0 and 1 can be read as a probability. That is why the sigmoid is the standard last step of a network that answers a yes/no question.

12.3 The algebra the lecturer left for you

The lecturer says "I'll leave the algebra to the reader". Here it is, in full. Start from the general objective of Chapter 11:

J(θ, w) = 𝔼px[ σf( Vw(x) ) ] − 𝔼pθ[ f*( σf( Vw(x) ) ) ]

To keep things tidy, write v for Vw(x), and define a new symbol:

Dw(x) = 11 + e−Vw(x)    (the sigmoid of the network's output)

First term. We need σf(v). Use the log rule "−log a = log(1/a)", which follows from fact 4 of Chapter 7.

σf(v) = −log( 1 + e−v ) definition
         = log 11 + e−v −log a = log(1/a)
         = log Dw(x) that fraction is exactly Dw

Second term. We need f*( σf(v) ). We just found σf(v) = log Dw. Put that in as t, and use the fact that e and log undo each other, so elog D = D.

f*( σf(v) ) = −log( 1 − elog Dw ) f*(t) = −log(1 − et) with t = log Dw
                 = −log( 1 − Dw(x) ) e and log cancel

Put both back. The second term of J has a minus sign in front, and we have just found another minus inside. Minus times minus is plus.

The GAN objective

JGAN(θ, w) = 𝔼px[ log Dw(x) ] + 𝔼pθ[ log( 1 − Dw(x) ) ]

A quick numeric check of the two steps. Suppose the network outputs v = 1.3 for some sample. Then Dw = sigmoid(1.3) = 0.786.

  • σf(1.3) = −log(1 + e−1.3) = −0.241, and log 0.786 = −0.241. Same.
  • f*(−0.241) = −log(1 − e−0.241) = 1.541, and −log(1 − 0.786) = −log 0.214 = 1.541. Same.

12.4 Meet the discriminator

The new symbol Dw(x) is called the discriminator. It is the network Vw followed by a sigmoid, so its output is always between 0 and 1.

A network that outputs one number between 0 and 1 is a binary classifier: a machine that sorts things into two classes. Here the natural reading is "the probability that this sample is real". An output of 0.95 says "almost surely real". An output of 0.03 says "almost surely fake". This is our detective.

The lecturer adds two clarifications:

  • The letter D is introduced only to match the notation of the original GAN paper.
  • Dw is not the function T itself. Do not confuse the discriminator's output range, 0 to 1, with dom f*, which is the negative numbers. The link is Tw(x) = σf(Vw(x)) = log Dw(x). The log of a number between 0 and 1 is negative, so all is consistent. By training Dw we are training T indirectly.

Common confusion: three different D's

Sadly, the letter D is used for three things in this subject. D alone (Chapter 2) is the dataset. Df( · ‖ · ) with a double bar is a divergence. Dw(x) with a subscript w and a sample inside is the discriminator. Look at what comes right after the letter and you will always know which one is meant.

Try it

1. The network Vw outputs v = 2 for a photo. What is Dw? Does the discriminator think it is real or fake?
2. What does Dw(x) = 0.5 mean?
3. If Dw(x) = 0.5, what is Tw(x)? Is it inside dom f*?
4. For the GAN's f, what is the smallest possible value of Df, and when is it reached?

Show answer

1. sigmoid(2) = 0.881. It thinks the photo is probably real.   2. The discriminator cannot decide. Real and fake look equally likely to it.   3. log 0.5 = −0.693. Yes, it is negative.   4. −log 4 = −1.386, reached when px = pθ (so that the JS divergence is 0).

Chapter 12 recap

  • A GAN is variational divergence minimisation with f(u) = u log u − (u+1) log(u+1), which gives 2 DJS − log 4.
  • With f*(t) = −log(1 − et) and σf(v) = −log(1 + e−v), the objective becomes JGAN = 𝔼px[log Dw(x)] + 𝔼pθ[log(1 − Dw(x))].
  • Dw(x) = sigmoid of Vw(x): a binary classifier giving the probability that x is real.
  • Tw = log Dw.

13.title: Reading the GAN scorecard
body:
We have the formula. Now we learn to read it like a scoreboard, with real numbers, and get it ready for a computer.

13.1 The objective, written out fully

JGAN(θ, w) = 𝔼x ~ px[ log Dw(x) ]  +  𝔼x̂ ~ pθ[ log( 1 − Dw(x̂) ) ]
PieceMeaning
𝔼x ~ pxAverage over real samples
log Dw(x)Log of the detective's "real" score for a real sample
𝔼x̂ ~ pθAverage over generated samples x̂ = gθ(z)
log( 1 − Dw(x̂) )Log of the detective's "fake" score for a generated sample. (If the chance of "real" is D, the chance of "fake" is 1 − D)

13.2 How log behaves between 0 and 1

a0.990.90.70.50.30.10.01
log a−0.010−0.105−0.357−0.693−1.204−2.303−4.605

For numbers between 0 and 1, the log is never positive. Near 1 it is close to 0. Near 0 it plunges to hugely negative values. So each term of JGAN acts like a mark out of zero: 0 is full marks, and anything more negative is worse.

13.3 What each player wants

The discriminator wants JGAN as large as possible (the "max over w"). The largest either term can be is 0.

  • First term near 0 needs Dw(x) near 1 for real samples: "call the real ones real".
  • Second term near 0 needs Dw(x̂) near 0 for generated samples: "call the fake ones fake".

That is exactly the job of a good detective.

The generator wants JGAN as small as possible (the "min over θ"). The generator has no say in the first term, since real photos do not pass through it. It can only influence the second term, through x̂. To make log(1 − Dw(x̂)) very negative it needs Dw(x̂) near 1: "make the detective call my fakes real".

That is exactly the job of a good forger. The story of Chapter 12 and the formula say the same thing.

13.4 The scorecard with numbers

Take three real photos and three generated ones. The table shows the discriminator's outputs in four situations, and the resulting score. For each situation, the first term is the average of the logs of the real-photo scores, and the second term is the average of log(1 − score) for the fakes.

SituationDw on 3 realDw on 3 fakeFirst termSecond termJGAN
Near-perfect detective0.99, 0.99, 0.990.01, 0.01, 0.01−0.010−0.010−0.020
Good detective0.9, 0.8, 0.70.2, 0.1, 0.3−0.228−0.228−0.457
Detective can only guess0.5, 0.5, 0.50.5, 0.5, 0.5−0.693−0.693−1.386
Detective fooled by the fakes0.9, 0.8, 0.70.6, 0.7, 0.8−0.228−1.243−1.472

Work one row by hand to be sure. "Good detective", first term: (log 0.9 + log 0.8 + log 0.7) ÷ 3 = (−0.105 − 0.223 − 0.357) ÷ 3 = −0.228. Second term: (log 0.8 + log 0.9 + log 0.7) ÷ 3 = −0.228. Total −0.457.

Now read the table from top to bottom. As the fakes get harder to catch, JGAN falls. The discriminator pushes towards the top rows. The generator drags towards the bottom rows.

And look at the highlighted row. When the detective can only guess, saying 0.5 for everything, the score is −1.386, which is −log 4. That is the very number from Chapter 12: the smallest value the GAN's divergence can take, reached when px = pθ. This is no accident. If the generated data follows the same distribution as the real data, no detective can do better than guessing. Part 3 looks at this link closely.

Common confusion: "the generator sees the real photos"

It never does. Real photos go only into the discriminator. Everything the generator learns about real data reaches it second-hand, through the discriminator's verdicts on its fakes.

13.5 What the two networks are made of

Both are ordinary neural networks, and the designer is free to choose the kind: an MLP (also called FNN), a CNN, and so on. The generator takes noise and outputs something with the shape of the data. The discriminator takes something with the shape of the data and outputs one number in [0, 1].

13.6 From expectations to something a computer can add up

The formula still has two expectations, and expectations need the unknown densities. Chapter 9 gave us the cure: the law of large numbers. Replace each expectation by an average over samples.

We do not use the whole dataset at once. We use a small handful at a time, called a batch:

  • pick B1 real samples x1, …, xB1 from the dataset (so they are samples of px),
  • draw B2 noise vectors z1, …, zB2 and compute x̂j = gθ(zj) (so they are samples of pθ).
JGAN(θ, w) ≈ 1B1 Σi=1B1 log Dw(xi)  +  1B2 Σj=1B2 log( 1 − Dw(x̂j) )

This is exactly what we did by hand in the scorecard, with B1 = B2 = 3. Every symbol on the right can now be computed: run samples through the networks, take logs, average. No unknown density is left anywhere.

Try it

1. A discriminator gives 0.9 to both of two real photos and 0.1 to both of two fakes. Find JGAN. (log 0.9 = −0.105)
2. The generator improves and the same discriminator now gives 0.5 to the fakes. Find the new JGAN. Did it move the way the generator wants?
3. Which term of JGAN does not depend on θ at all?
4. Can JGAN ever be positive?

Show answer

1. First term −0.105. Second term: log(1 − 0.1) = log 0.9 = −0.105. Total −0.210.   2. Second term becomes log 0.5 = −0.693. Total −0.798. Yes, it went down.   3. The first term, which involves only real samples.   4. No. Both terms are logs of numbers between 0 and 1, so each is at most 0.

Chapter 13 recap

  • JGAN = 𝔼x~px log Dw(x) + 𝔼x̂~pθ log(1 − Dw(x̂)). Its largest possible value is 0.
  • The discriminator raises it by scoring real near 1 and fake near 0.
  • The generator lowers it by making fakes that score near 1.
  • When the detective can only guess, JGAN = −log 4.
  • In practice both expectations are replaced by averages over batches of B1 real and B2 generated samples.

14.title: How a GAN is trained
body:
We know what each network wants. This chapter shows how the knobs are actually turned, one small step at a time.

The problem

In Chapter 5 we found the best knob by trying seven values in a table. A real network has crores of knobs. Trying all combinations is impossible. We need a way to improve all the knobs a little at a time, knowing only which direction is "better".

Detour: walking downhill (gradient descent)

You are on a hillside in thick fog and want to reach the valley. You cannot see the valley. But you can feel the slope under your feet. So you take a small step in the downhill direction, feel the slope again, and repeat.

The slope of a curve at a point says how fast the height changes when you move a little to the right. Positive slope: going right takes you up. Negative slope: going right takes you down. Zero slope: you are on flat ground, such as the bottom of a valley.

Take one knob w and a "height" J(w) = (w − 3)², a bowl with its bottom at w = 3. Its slope at any point is 2(w − 3). (That formula comes from calculus, which you will learn in Class 11. But you can check it yourself. At w = 0 the height is 9. Move a tiny bit right, to w = 0.01: the height is 2.99² = 8.9401. The height changed by −0.0599 over a step of 0.01, which is a slope of about −5.99. The formula says 2(0 − 3) = −6. It matches. It also makes sense in general: left of 3 the slope is negative, right of 3 it is positive, and at 3 it is zero.)

The rule for one step downhill is:

new w = old w − α × slope

The number α (alpha) is the step size, a small positive number we choose. The minus sign does the right thing by itself: if the slope is positive we move left, and if it is negative we move right. Either way, downhill. Start at w = 0 with α = 0.25:

StepwHeight (w − 3)²Slope 2(w − 3)New w = w − 0.25 × slope
009−60 + 1.5 = 1.5
11.52.25−31.5 + 0.75 = 2.25
22.250.5625−1.52.25 + 0.375 = 2.625
32.6250.1406−0.752.8125
42.81250.0352−0.3752.90625

The knob walks towards 3 by itself. This method is called gradient descent, and it is how nearly every neural network is trained.

  • Step size matters. Too small and progress is painfully slow. Too large and you jump over the valley: with α = 1.1 the same start gives 0 → 6.6 → −1.32 → 8.18, getting worse every step.
  • Many knobs. With many knobs there is one slope per knob. The whole list of slopes is called the gradient, written with an upside-down triangle: ∇w J ("the gradient of J with respect to the knobs w"). The rule is the same, applied to all knobs together. Example with two knobs: let J(a, b) = (a − 1)² + (b + 2)², a bowl whose bottom is at a = 1, b = −2. The slopes are 2(a − 1) and 2(b + 2). At the start (0, 0) the gradient is (−2, 4). With α = 0.25: new a = 0 − 0.25 × (−2) = 0.5, and new b = 0 − 0.25 × 4 = −1. Both knobs have moved towards the bottom in one step.
  • Climbing instead. If you want to go up, to maximise, flip the sign to a plus: new w = old w + α × slope. This is gradient ascent. Example: the hill J(w) = −(w − 3)² has its top at w = 3 and slope −2(w − 3). At w = 0 the slope is 6, so new w = 0 + 0.25 × 6 = 1.5. It has moved towards the top.

Detour: three training words

  • Forward propagation: feed inputs into the network and compute the outputs, layer by layer, front to back.
  • Backward propagation (backprop): the method by which the computer works out the gradient, the slope for every knob. It starts from the final score and works backwards through the layers, finding how much each knob is responsible. You do not need its details here. The software does it automatically.
  • Epoch: we train on one small batch at a time and take one gradient step per batch. Going through the whole dataset once, batch after batch, is called one epoch. Training runs for many epochs. This way of working is called batch gradient descent.

14.1 The plan: take turns

We need argminθ maxw JGAN(θ, w). The two networks are trained alternately: freeze one, improve the other a little, then swap. Just like the forger and the detective taking turns to learn.

14.2 Turn A: train the discriminator (generator frozen)

Keep θ constant. We want

w* = argmaxw [ 𝔼px log Dw(x) + 𝔼pθ log( 1 − Dw(x̂) ) ]

(argmax is the twin of argmin: the setting that gives the largest value. If J is 2, 5 and 3 at w = 1, 2 and 3, then the max is 5 and the argmax is 2.) Step by step:

  1. Pick a batch of B1 real samples from the dataset: {x1, …, xB1} ⊂ D. (⊂ means "is a part of".)
  2. Sample z1, …, zB2 ~ N(0, I) and pass them through the generator, with its knobs fixed, to get fakes gθ(z1), …, gθ(zB2).
  3. Forward propagation: send both the real batch and the fake batch through the discriminator and compute
    JGAN = 1B1 Σi log Dw(xi) + 1B2 Σj log( 1 − Dw( gθ(zj) ) )
  4. Backward propagation: compute the gradient ∇w JGAN.
  5. Take one step uphill:
    wt+1 ← wt + α1 ∇w JGAN(θ, w)

In that last line, wt means "the knobs after t steps" (the small t is a step counter, not a power), the arrow ← means "is replaced by", and α1 is the discriminator's step size.

The lecturer points out the plus sign. Most machine learning problems are minimisations and use gradient descent with a minus. Here the discriminator is maximising, so it does gradient ascent.

14.3 Turn B: train the generator (discriminator frozen)

Keep w constant. We want θ* = argminθ JGAN(θ, w). Write out the batch version:

argminθ [ 1B1 Σi log Dw(xi) + 1B2 Σj log( 1 − Dw(x̂j) ) ]

The first sum involves only real samples and the frozen discriminator. It has no θ in it. Whatever we do to the generator, that sum stays the same, so it cannot affect which θ is best. We can ignore it. What remains:

θ* ≈ argminθ 1B2 Σj=1B2 log( 1 − Dw( gθ(zj) ) )

An important consequence, which the lecturer states directly: real data is not needed at all while training the generator. Step by step:

  1. Sample z1, …, zB2 ~ N(0, I).
  2. Forward propagation: pass them through the generator, then pass the fakes through the frozen discriminator, and compute the average of log(1 − Dw(gθ(zj))).
  3. Backward propagation: compute ∇θ JGAN. The blame travels backwards through the discriminator and into the generator. The discriminator's knobs are not changed on this turn. They only pass the message along.
  4. Take one step downhill:
    θt+1 ← θt − α2 ∇θ JGAN(θ, w)

Here α2 is the generator's step size, and the sign is a minus because the generator is minimising.

Turn A: discriminatorTurn B: generator
Knobs updatedwθ
Knobs frozenθw
Goalmake JGAN largermake JGAN smaller
Methodgradient ascent (+)gradient descent (−)
Needs real data?YesNo
Needs noise z?YesYes
Terms of JGAN usedbothonly the second

14.4 The whole algorithm on one page

Training a GAN

Input: a dataset D = {x1, …, xn} drawn iid from px. Nothing else.

Start: set both networks' knobs θ and w to random values.

Repeat for many epochs, batch by batch:

  1. Discriminator turn. Take a real batch and a freshly generated fake batch. Compute JGAN. Update w ← w + α1 ∇w JGAN, keeping θ fixed.
  2. Generator turn. Generate a fake batch. Compute the second term of JGAN. Update θ ← θ − α2 ∇θ JGAN, keeping w fixed.

Afterwards: to create new data, draw z ~ N(0, I) and compute gθ*(z), exactly as in Chapter 6.

The lecturer notes that this same procedure trains any model of the variational-divergence-minimisation family, not only the GAN. Only the formula for J changes with the choice of f.

14.5 Looking back at the four questions

#Question from Chapter 6Answer so far
1How to compute a divergence without knowing the densities?Use the variational lower bound. It needs only sample averages
2Which divergence?For the GAN, a close relative of JS. Part 4 tries another
3How to design the networks?Any neural networks so far. Part 3 gives designs made for images
4How to solve the optimisation?Alternate gradient ascent on the discriminator with gradient descent on the generator

Try it

1. For J(w) = (w − 3)², start at w = 5 with α = 0.25. Find w after one step and after two steps.
2. Why is there a plus sign in the discriminator's update and a minus sign in the generator's?
3. During the generator's turn, the gradient passes through the discriminator. Do the discriminator's knobs change?
4. A dataset has 10,000 photos and the batch size is 100. How many discriminator steps are in one epoch?

Show answer

1. Slope at 5 is 2(5 − 3) = 4, so w = 5 − 0.25 × 4 = 4. Slope at 4 is 2, so w = 4 − 0.5 = 3.5. It is approaching 3 from the right.   2. The discriminator maximises JGAN (ascent, plus). The generator minimises it (descent, minus).   3. No. On that turn w is held constant.   4. 10,000 ÷ 100 = 100 steps.

Chapter 14 recap, and the end of Part 2

  • Gradient descent: new knob = old knob − step size × slope. Ascent uses a plus.
  • A GAN is trained by alternating: one ascent step on w, one descent step on θ.
  • The generator's turn uses only log(1 − Dw(gθ(z))) and needs no real data.
  • The whole of Part 2 in one sentence: choose a JS-like f, represent the helper function by a classifier network, and the lower bound of Part 1 becomes a game between a forger and a detective, played with alternating gradient steps.
Coming next: Part 3, Chapters 15 to 17. Why a classifier is the right guide for a generator, how to build both networks for images, and how to tell a GAN which picture to draw.

15.title: The GAN, seen as a classifier that guides a generator
body:
Forget divergences for one chapter. We start again from nothing but a generator and a classifier, and arrive at exactly the same place.

Starting fresh

We have the dataset D = {x1, …, xn} drawn iid from px, and a generator gθ whose outputs x̂ follow pθ. The goal has not changed: bring pθ close to px.

Now suppose somebody hands us a binary classifier Dw(x) that looks at a sample and answers:

Dw(x) = 1 if x came from px (real),    0 if x came from pθ (generated)

The lecturer's question: can this classifier be used to make pθ and px closer?

15.1 A first idea: make the classifier fail

If the generated samples were distributed exactly like the real ones, no classifier could separate them. There would be nothing to go on. In symbols:

px = pθ  ⟹  the classifier fails

(The arrow ⟹ is read "implies".) This suggests a simple plan: keep adjusting the generator's knobs θ until the classifier can no longer tell real from generated.

15.2 Why the first idea is not enough

There is a trap. The arrow above points one way only. Turning it around is not valid:

the classifier fails  ⇏  px = pθ

A fixed classifier can be fooled without the two distributions becoming equal. Here is a counter-example in one dimension. (The lecturer draws the same idea with clusters of points in two dimensions.) Suppose the real data are heights of students, all between 150 and 160 cm.

RoundWhere the fakes areThe classifier's ruleWhat happens
1100 to 110Rule 1: "real if above 130"Works perfectly. The generator must move
2185 to 195still Rule 1The fakes are above 130, so Rule 1 calls them real. The classifier fails. But 185–195 is nothing like 150–160
3185 to 195new Rule 2: "real if below 175"The classifier works again. The generator must move again
4135 to 145Rules 1 and 2 are both fooledCloser, but still not equal. A third rule, "real if above 147", catches it

In round 2 the generator "won" against the fixed classifier while being completely wrong. A fixed classifier checks only one thing, and the generator needs to satisfy only that one thing.

The cure is visible in the table. Every time the generator escapes, retrain the classifier so that it separates real from generated again. Each new rule closes one more escape route, and the fakes are squeezed closer and closer to the real data. The lecturer's conclusion:

The lesson

The classifier must not be fixed. It has to be changed simultaneously, along with the generator.

15.3 Writing down what the classifier wants

Let the classifier give a number between 0 and 1, in symbols Dw : 𝒳 → [0, 1], and let Dw(x) stand for the likelihood that the sample x came from px, that is, that it is real.

Detour: likelihood and log-likelihood

Likelihood is how probable the right answer is, according to the model. Suppose a photo is real. A classifier that says "90% real" gives the truth a likelihood of 0.9. One that says "20% real" gives the truth a likelihood of only 0.2. A good classifier is one that gives high likelihood to what is actually true. Training a classifier means adjusting its knobs to maximise the likelihood. The lecturer notes that this is the objective of any classifier.

In practice people maximise the log of the likelihood, the log-likelihood. Nothing is lost by this: the log is an always-rising function, so whatever makes the likelihood bigger also makes its log bigger. (Look back at the log table in Chapter 7: as u grows, log u grows.) And something is gained: the log turns multiplication into addition (fact 3 of Chapter 7), so the likelihoods of many samples can simply be averaged.

Example. A classifier gives three real photos the scores 0.9, 0.8 and 0.7. The likelihood of getting all three right is the product, 0.9 × 0.8 × 0.7 = 0.504. Now take logs and add: −0.105 − 0.223 − 0.357 = −0.685. And log 0.504 = −0.685. The sum of the logs carries exactly the same information as the product, and is much easier to work with.

Job 1: say "real" for real samples. Maximise the log-likelihood that real samples came from px:

w* = argmaxw 𝔼x~px[ log Dw(x) ]

Job 2: say "not real" for generated samples. If Dw(x̂) is the likelihood that x̂ is real, then 1 − Dw(x̂) is the likelihood that it is not real. For generated samples that is the truth, so maximise its log too:

w* = argmaxw 𝔼x̂~pθ[ log( 1 − Dw(x̂) ) ]

Both jobs together. Add the two:

w* = argmaxw { 𝔼x~px[ log Dw(x) ] + 𝔼x̂~pθ[ log( 1 − Dw(x̂) ) ] }  =  argmaxw J(θ, w)

15.4 Writing down what the generator wants

The generator's aim is that the classifier should fail. The classifier succeeds by making J large. So the generator does the opposite. The lecturer's phrase is "invert the optimisation for the classifier":

θ* = argminθ J(θ, w)

Put the two together, with the classifier being retrained all along as Section 15.2 demands:

θ*, w* = arg minθ maxw J(θ, w)

This is an adversarial optimisation. And look at J. It is exactly JGAN from Chapter 12.

15.5 Two roads, one destination

Road 1 (Parts 1 and 2)Road 2 (this chapter)
Starting ideaMinimise a divergence between px and pθMake a classifier unable to tell real from generated
Why two networks?The second network represents the function T in the lower boundThe second network is the classifier
Why train both together?The bound is tight only if T keeps being maximisedA fixed classifier can be fooled without matching the data
Final formulaargminθ maxw [ 𝔼 log Dw(x) + 𝔼 log(1 − Dw(x̂)) ]

The lecturer calls this view the GAN as a classifier-guided generative sampler: a sampler (the generator) that is steered by a classifier. Road 2 is quick and easy to remember. Road 1 is longer, but it tells us what is being minimised (a JS-like divergence), which Road 2 alone does not. That knowledge is what lets us diagnose and repair GANs in Part 4.

It also explains the −log 4 we noticed in Chapter 13. If px = pθ, the best any classifier can do is answer 0.5 for everything, and then J = log 0.5 + log 0.5 = −log 4.

Try it

1. In the heights example, the fakes are at 135–145. Give one rule that still separates them from the real data (150–160).
2. True or false: "If a classifier cannot separate real from generated samples, the generator must be perfect."
3. A real photo gets Dw = 0.8. What likelihood does the classifier give to the truth? What if the photo was actually generated?
4. Why do we maximise the log-likelihood and not the likelihood itself?

Show answer

1. "Real if above 147" (anything between 145 and 150 works).   2. False. That particular classifier may simply be checking the wrong thing. A retrained classifier might separate them easily.   3. 0.8 if it is real. If it was generated, the truth is "not real", which gets 1 − 0.8 = 0.2.   4. Both have their maximum at the same place, and logs turn products into sums, which are easy to average.

Chapter 15 recap

  • Idea: adjust the generator until a classifier cannot tell real from generated.
  • px = pθ ⟹ classifier fails, but classifier fails ⇏ px = pθ.
  • So the classifier must be retrained alongside the generator.
  • The classifier maximises the log-likelihood of labelling both kinds correctly. The generator minimises the same quantity.
  • The result is the same GAN objective as before.

16.title: A GAN built for pictures: DCGAN
body:
So far "any neural network will do". For images there is a better design, called the Deep Convolutional GAN.

The problem

The lecturer begins with a reminder: nothing we have done so far depends on the kind of data. The theory works for images, speech or text alike. But when the data are images, we can design the networks to suit them. This is the third question from Chapter 6: how should we choose gθ?

16.1 The shape of a generator: small in, big out

The noise z lives in ℝk and the data in ℝd. In a typical GAN, k is much smaller than d, written k ≪ d. For example, k might be 16 while d is 4,80,000.

So the generator has to grow its input. Layer by layer, the list of numbers gets longer: 16 → 32 → 64 → … → d. This is why the generator is always drawn as a shape that widens from left to right.

16.2 The plain way: an MLP, then reshape

With a multi-layer perceptron (MLP, also called a fully connected network), the final layer outputs one long flat list of d numbers. To see it as a picture, that list must be reshaped: cut into rows and stacked into a grid, the reverse of the flattening we did in Chapter 2.

This works, but it is wasteful. An MLP treats the output as a plain list. It has no idea that number 5 and number 6 are neighbouring pixels, or that number 5 and number 405 sit one above the other. It must discover all of that from scratch.

Detour: convolution, the image-friendly layer

In a picture, nearby pixels belong together: they form edges, corners, eyes, whiskers. A convolutional layer is built around this fact. Instead of connecting everything to everything, it slides a small window, called a filter, across the image. At each position it multiplies the pixels under the window by the filter's numbers and adds them up. The filter's numbers are the knobs that are learnt.

Example. A 4 × 4 image and a 2 × 2 filter:

imagefilter
120110
013101

1012

Place the filter on the top-left 2 × 2 corner, which holds 1, 2 / 0, 1. Multiply matching positions and add: 1×1 + 2×0 + 0×0 + 1×1 = 2. Slide one step right, onto 2, 0 / 1, 3: 2×1 + 0×0 + 1×0 + 3×1 = 5. Continue over all nine positions:

output (3 × 3)
251
