222

Two things to notice. The same small filter is reused everywhere, so a pattern is detected wherever it appears in the picture, with very few knobs. And the output (3 × 3) is smaller than the input (4 × 4). Ordinary convolutions shrink pictures, which suits a network that goes from a big image to a small answer. A network made of such layers is a CNN, a convolutional neural network.

Detour: transpose convolution, the layer that enlarges

A generator needs the opposite: start small and grow. The layer for this is the transpose convolution, also called up-convolution. The idea is reversed. Each input number is multiplied by the whole filter, and the result is stamped onto the output as a block.

Example. A 2 × 2 input and a 2 × 2 filter, with the stamps placed side by side:

inputfilteroutput (4 × 4)
12121224
01343468
0012
0034

The top-left input, 1, stamps 1 × filter into the top-left block. The top-right input, 2, stamps 2 × filter (2, 4 / 6, 8) into the top-right block. The 0 stamps a block of zeros, and the last 1 stamps the filter itself. A 2 × 2 grid has become a 4 × 4 grid. Stack several such layers and a tiny grid grows into a full picture: 4 × 4 → 8 × 8 → 16 × 16 → 32 × 32 → 64 × 64.

16.3 The DCGAN design

In a Deep Convolutional GAN (DCGAN), the generator is built from transpose convolution (up-convolution) layers. It starts from a small z, say in ℝ16, and each layer enlarges it, until the final layer has exactly the shape of the data: rows × columns × 3 colour channels. In symbols, x ∈ ℝr × c × 3.

MLP generatorDCGAN generator
LayersFully connectedTranspose convolutions
Output of the last layerA flat list of d numbersA grid of shape r × c × 3
Reshaping needed?YesNo. The output is already an image
Knows that pixels have neighbours?NoYes, by design
Used forAny dataImages

The lecture's focus is on the generator. In practice the discriminator of a DCGAN is also convolutional, using ordinary (shrinking) convolutions to go from an image down to a single number. That fits what we saw in the first detour.

Common confusion: DCGAN is not a new theory

The objective is the same JGAN. The training is the same alternating procedure of Chapter 14. Only the insides of the networks have changed. DCGAN is an answer to "how should we build gθ for images?", nothing more.

Try it

1. Using the 4 × 4 image and filter from the first detour, check the bottom-right output value by hand.
2. A 5 × 5 image and a 2 × 2 filter, sliding one step at a time: what size is the output?
3. In the transpose convolution example, what would the top-right block be if the top-right input were 3?
4. Why does a DCGAN generator not need a reshape step?

Show answer

1. The window covers 0, 0 / 1, 2. So 0×1 + 0×0 + 1×0 + 2×1 = 2.   2. 4 × 4. (The window fits in 4 positions across and 4 down.)   3. 3 × filter = 3, 6 / 9, 12.   4. Because its last layer already outputs a grid with the image's shape, r × c × 3.

Chapter 16 recap

  • A generator turns a small noise vector into large data: k ≪ d.
  • An MLP outputs a flat list that must be reshaped into an image.
  • Convolution slides a small filter over a grid. Transpose convolution does the reverse and enlarges the grid.
  • DCGAN = a GAN whose generator uses transpose convolutions, so its output is directly an image. The objective and training are unchanged.

17.title: Telling the GAN what to draw: conditional GANs
body:
Our GAN makes pictures, but we have no say in which picture. This chapter adds a steering wheel.

The problem

You train a GAN on photos of many kinds of animals. It works. You press the button and get… a horse. Press again: a cat. Again: a parrot. You wanted a dog.

The lecturer puts it this way: so far our sampling has been unconditional. Once the generator is trained, there is no way to control what it produces. In real use we want an image of a particular class, or one matching a particular description. Remember the word "conditional" from Chapter 1? Here is how it is done.

17.1 New data: every example comes with a label

To teach "what a dog is", the dataset must say which photos are dogs. So each example is now a pair:

D = { (x1, y1), (x2, y2), … , (xn, yn) }  ~  iid  ℙxy
  • xi is the image.
  • yi is the information that goes with it: a class label ("dog"), or a textual embedding, which is a written description of the image converted into a vector of numbers. The lecturer says not to worry about how embeddings are made yet. That comes later in the course. Here we stick to class labels.

The lecturer points out that this is the very kind of data a discriminative model (a judge, in Chapter 1's words) is trained on: examples with labels.

Detour: joint and conditional distributions

When each example has two parts, we need two new ideas. To keep the numbers small, imagine each photo is described by just one feature: is the animal sitting or running? And there are two labels, cat and dog.

The joint distribution pxy gives the probability of every combination:

Joint probabilitysittingrunningRow total
cat0.300.100.40
dog0.150.450.60
Column total0.450.551

All four cells add to 1. The totals in the margins are the distributions of each part taken alone: 45% of all photos are "sitting", 40% of all photos are cats. These are called marginal distributions, because they sit in the margins of the table. The px we have used all along is such a marginal: the distribution of images when labels are ignored.

The conditional distribution answers a narrower question: among cats only, how are the photos distributed? Take the cat row and divide by its total:

sittingrunningTotal
p(x | y = cat)0.30 ÷ 0.40 = 0.750.10 ÷ 0.40 = 0.251
p(x | y = dog)0.15 ÷ 0.60 = 0.250.45 ÷ 0.60 = 0.751

The bar "|" is read "given", as in Chapter 4. So px|y is "the distribution of images, given the label". Notice how different the three are: overall, 45% of photos are sitting. Given "cat", 75% are. Given "dog", only 25% are. The condition changes the distribution.

17.2 The new goal

Unconditional GANConditional GAN
Sample fromthe marginal pxthe conditional px|y
In words"Give me an image""Give me an image of a dog"

The lecturer's good news: "thankfully nothing changes in the formulation". The solution is the old recipe with one substitution: estimate px|y in place of px, and make the model distribution approach px|y, for every y. To do this, modify the generator and the discriminator so that both operate on samples of the conditional distribution. In practice: give the label to both of them as an extra input.

Detour: one-hot encoding

A network eats numbers, and "dog" is a word. We could number the classes cat = 1, dog = 2, horse = 3, but that wrongly suggests that horse is "three times cat" or that dog lies "between" cat and horse. The standard fix is one-hot encoding: with K classes, use a list of K numbers that is all zeros except for a single 1 at the position of the class.

ClassOne-hot vector
cat[1, 0, 0]
dog[0, 1, 0]
horse[0, 0, 1]

"One-hot" because exactly one position is switched on.

17.3 The conditional GAN

The generator now receives two inputs: the noise z ~ N(0, I) and the label y as a one-hot vector. Its output is a sample from the model's conditional distribution, which the lectures write as x̂ | y ~ pθx̂|y. The label says what to draw. The noise decides which particular one, so different z with the same y give different dogs.

The discriminator also receives two inputs: an image (real x or generated x̂) and the label y. Its question changes from "is this image real?" to "is this a real image of this class?".

The objective is the GAN objective with y added inside:

J(θ, w) = 𝔼x, y ~ px|y[ log Dw(x, y) ] + 𝔼x̂, y ~ pθx̂|y[ log( 1 − Dw(x̂, y) ) ]

Example. Suppose the label is "dog". A well-trained conditional discriminator might answer like this:

Image shownLabel shownDw(image, label)Why
A real dog photodog0.9Real, and matches the label
A blurry generated dogdog0.2Matches the label but does not look real
A sharp generated catdog0.05Looks real, but is not a dog

The first row feeds the term log Dw(x, y): log 0.9 = −0.105. The other two feed log(1 − Dw(x̂, y)): log 0.8 = −0.223 and log 0.95 = −0.051.

Training is the same alternating procedure as in Chapter 14.

Common confusion: "only the generator needs the label"

If the discriminator did not see y, it could only check whether an image looks real. The generator could then ignore the label completely and draw a lovely cat when asked for a dog, and never be caught. Because the discriminator sees the pair (image, label), a real-looking cat labelled "dog" is flagged as fake, since no such pair exists in the real data. That is what forces the generator to obey the label.

17.4 Using a trained GAN: inference

The lecturer closes the topic with something he calls "pretty trivial" but worth stating: how to actually use a GAN once training is over. This step is called inference. For a generative model, inference simply means generating data.

Inference with a GAN

Input: a trained generator gθ*, obtained by solving the min–max problem.

Steps: draw a fresh noise vector ztest ~ N(0, I). For a conditional GAN, also choose the label y you want. Pass them through the generator.

Output: xtest = gθ*(ztest, y), a sample from the data distribution that corresponds to the class y, and which (we hope) is not present in the dataset D.

Two things to notice. Only the generator is used at this stage. The discriminator did its work during training. And the output should be a new sample, not a copy of a training example. That was the point of the whole exercise, right from Riya's poem in Chapter 1.

Try it

1. From the joint table in the detour, what fraction of all photos are "dog and sitting"? Among dogs only, what fraction are sitting?
2. Write the one-hot vector for the class "horse" when the classes are, in order: cat, dog, horse, parrot.
3. You run a trained conditional GAN twice with the same y but different z. What do you expect?
4. You run it twice with the same z and the same y. What do you expect? (Hint: Chapter 6 said the generator is deterministic.)

Show answer

1. 0.15 of all photos. Among dogs: 0.15 ÷ 0.60 = 0.25.   2. [0, 0, 1, 0].   3. Two different images of the same class.   4. Exactly the same image both times. All the variety comes from the noise.

Chapter 17 recap, and the end of Part 3

  • An unconditional GAN samples from px with no control over what comes out.
  • A conditional GAN (cGAN) is trained on pairs (x, y) and samples from px|y.
  • The label y (one-hot) is given to both the generator and the discriminator.
  • J = 𝔼 log Dw(x, y) + 𝔼 log(1 − Dw(x̂, y)).
  • Inference: draw z, choose y, run the trained generator.
Coming next: Part 4, Chapters 18 to 22. Why GAN training often gets stuck, a different kind of distance that fixes it, how to run a GAN backwards, a use of the adversarial idea that has nothing to do with generating, and how to give a generator marks.

18.title: Why GAN training gets stuck
body:
On paper the GAN is beautiful. In practice it is famous for being hard to train. This chapter finds one deep reason.

The problem

People who train GANs often see this: the discriminator quickly becomes excellent, catching every fake, and then the generator simply stops improving. In the forger story, the detective is now so sharp that every note is rejected instantly, and the rejections carry no hint about what to fix. A teacher who writes only "0/10, all wrong" on every answer sheet teaches nothing.

The lecturer names two sources of trouble. First, a saddle point is simply harder to find than an ordinary minimum. Second, and deeper: f-divergence minimisation itself leads to unstable training. All GANs of this family start from an f-divergence, build a lower bound, and minimise it. The question is what makes this unstable.

18.1 Real data fills almost none of its space

Do this experiment, taken from the lecture. Take a grid of 28 × 28 pixels. For each pixel toss a coin: heads, colour it black (1); tails, leave it white (0). You get a random black-and-white image.

How many different images can this produce? Each of the 784 pixels has 2 choices, so 2784 images. That is a number with 237 digits. The set of all of them is written {0, 1}784.

And how likely is it that your random image looks like a letter of the alphabet, or a digit, or anything meaningful? Practically zero. You will get speckled noise every time. The lecturer compares it to the old puzzle of a monkey hitting typewriter keys at random: what are the chances it types out Shakespeare?

So images that mean something are an unimaginably tiny part of all possible images. We met this idea as the "snow" in Chapter 4. Now it gets a name.

The manifold hypothesis

Distributions of real data (such as images) lie on a lower-dimensional manifold in the ambient space ℝd.

Three words to unpack:

  • Ambient space: the big space the data is written in. For our images, ℝd with d in the lakhs.
  • Manifold: the lecturer skips the rigorous definition and says to think of it as a lower-dimensional subspace sitting inside the ambient space. His examples: hold a sheet of paper in a room. The room is 3-dimensional, and every point on the paper needs 3 coordinates to describe, but the paper itself is a 2-dimensional surface. Or hold a thread of zero thickness: a 1-dimensional thing living in 3-dimensional space.
  • Hypothesis: it is a belief, not a proven fact. There is no way to test it for certain, but a great deal of practical evidence supports it.

So picture real images not as a cloud filling the room, but as a thin sheet floating in it.

18.2 Two thin sheets almost never line up

Recall the word support from Chapter 7: the region where a distribution actually puts its probability. By the manifold hypothesis, the support of px is a thin sheet in ℝd. The generated data also lies on a thin sheet. That is natural, since the generator stretches a small k-dimensional noise into the big space, like bending a sheet.

Now toss two sheets of paper into a room. What is the chance that they land exactly on top of each other? Essentially none. At best they cross along a line. In the same way, the lecturer says, the supports of px and pθ will not be aligned, with very high probability.

18.3 Then a perfect detective exists

If the real sheet and the fake sheet do not overlap, a classifier only has to learn "which sheet is this point on?". The lecture states the result, known as the perfect discriminator theorem:

Perfect discriminator theorem

It can be shown that a perfect discriminator (a Dw with 100% accuracy) can be learned when the supports of px and pθ are not aligned.

When that happens, Df( px ‖ pθ ) becomes independent of the generator's parameters θ, and GAN training saturates.

18.4 Seeing saturation with numbers

Take the simplest "thin" distributions there are. All the real data sits at one point, position 0. All the generated data sits at one point, position θ. The generator's single knob slides its point along the number line. The goal is obviously θ = 0.

For any θ other than 0, the two do not overlap, and a perfect discriminator is trivial: "real if at 0, fake otherwise". Now compute the JS divergence for different θ. When two distributions share no outcome at all, JS always comes out as log 2 = 0.693, the largest value it can take.

Here is the working, using the midpoint form of JS from Chapter 8. The real distribution puts probability 1 at position 0. The fake one puts probability 1 at position θ. Their midpoint m puts 0.5 at each.

KL(real ‖ m) = 1 × log(1 ÷ 0.5) = log 2 = 0.693
KL(fake ‖ m) = 1 × log(1 ÷ 0.5) = log 2 = 0.693
JS = ½ × 0.693 + ½ × 0.693 = 0.693

The number θ does not appear anywhere in this working. That is the whole problem.

Generator's position θ10510.10.010
JS divergence0.6930.6930.6930.6930.6930
True gap |θ|10510.10.010

Look at the JS row. It is the same number everywhere except at the exact answer. The generator at 10 and the generator at 0.01 receive the same verdict. The divergence only reports whether the supports overlap. It says nothing about how far apart they are. This is what "independent of θ" means.

Now remember gradient descent from Chapter 14: new knob = old knob − step size × slope. On a flat line the slope is zero. Zero times anything is zero. The knob does not move. The generator is standing on a perfectly level plain in thick fog, with no downhill direction to feel. That is saturation.

It ties up with Chapter 13 too. With the GAN's own f, the divergence is 2 × JS − log 4 = 2 × 0.693 − 1.386 = 0. And 0 is the largest value JGAN can take, the score of a perfect detective.

Common confusion: "a stronger discriminator is always better"

In Chapter 11 we said the generator needs a sharp critic, and that is true. But with an f-divergence, a perfect critic gives a verdict with no direction in it. The trouble is not the critic. It is that the thing being measured, the f-divergence, has gone flat.

18.5 What to do about it

The lecturer mentions one practical remedy: do not train the generator and the discriminator equally, so that the discriminator does not get too far ahead. But this is a rule of thumb found by trial and error. Is there a cure that comes from reasoning?

Yes. Use a "softer" divergence: one that does not saturate when the supports do not align. It should not merely check whether the supports overlap. It should measure how far apart they are, like the bottom row of the table and the dashed green line in the figure. The next chapter builds exactly that.

Try it

1. How many different images can a 2 × 2 grid of black/white pixels show?
2. A string lies on your desk. What is the dimension of the string, and of the ambient space?
3. In the point example, the generator is at θ = 3, and gradient descent is run on the JS divergence. Where is the generator after 100 steps?
4. Why is "the true gap |θ|" a more useful signal than the JS row?

Show answer

1. 24 = 16.   2. The string is 1-dimensional. The ambient space is 3-dimensional (or 2, if you count only the desktop).   3. Still at 3. The slope is zero, so no step moves it.   4. Because it gets smaller as the generator gets closer, so it always has a slope pointing towards the answer.

Chapter 18 recap

  • Manifold hypothesis: real data lies on a thin, lower-dimensional sheet inside ℝd.
  • The supports of px and pθ are two thin sheets that almost surely do not align.
  • Then a perfect discriminator exists, the f-divergence stops depending on θ, and training saturates.
  • Cure: a softer divergence that measures how far, not just whether.

19.title: A distance that never goes flat: the Wasserstein GAN
body:
We replace the f-divergence with a distance based on a very down-to-earth idea: how much work it takes to move things.

A story about wheat

Two villages on a straight road have wheat in their godowns: one at the 0 km stone, one at the 10 km stone. Each holds half of all the wheat. Two towns need it: one at the 1 km stone and one at the 11 km stone, each needing half.

You own the lorry. Moving wheat costs effort: amount moved × distance moved. There are many ways to do the job. What is the least total effort?

That least effort is a sensible measure of how different the "where the wheat is" picture is from the "where the wheat is needed" picture. This is the idea behind the Wasserstein metric, also called optimal transport.

19.1 From wheat to distributions

Think of a distribution as a pile of mass spread over positions. Total mass: 1. In the lecture's words, the mass in px can be redistributed so that px gets converted into another distribution px̂.

Position 0Position 1Position 10Position 11
px (where the mass is)0.500.50
px̂ (where it should go)00.500.5

19.2 A transport plan is a joint distribution

A transport plan says how much mass goes from each starting position x to each final position x̂. Write it as a table, with one row per start and one column per destination. Here are three plans.

Plan Ato 1to 11Row totalPlan Bto 1to 11Row total
from 00.500.5from 000.50.5
from 1000.50.5from 100.500.5
Column total0.50.51Column total0.50.51
Plan Cto 1to 11Row total
from 00.250.250.5
from 100.250.250.5
Column total0.25 + 0.25 = 0.50.51

Does this kind of table look familiar? It is a joint distribution, just like the cat/dog table of Chapter 17. Every cell is a probability and all cells add to 1. And a plan is valid only if its margins come out right:

  • the row totals must equal px (you cannot ship more than a village has), and
  • the column totals must equal px̂ (each town must receive exactly what it needs).

The lecture writes a plan as a joint distribution γ(x, x̂) (γ is the Greek letter gamma) and the family of all valid plans as Π(x, x̂) (capital pi). The two margin conditions are written with integrals, which you can read as "add over":

∫x̂ γ(x, x̂) dx̂ = px     and     ∫x γ(x, x̂) dx = px̂

The lecturer sums it up: every redistribution scheme is a joint distribution, and is called a "transport plan".

19.3 The work done by a plan

SymbolMeaning
‖x − x̂‖The distance of the movement from x to x̂
γ(x, x̂)The amount of mass moved from x to x̂
γ(x, x̂) · ‖x − x̂‖The "work done" in moving that mass

Detour: the double bars ‖ ‖ mean length

For plain numbers, the distance between 3 and 7 is |3 − 7| = 4. For lists of numbers, the distance comes from Pythagoras' theorem. Between the points (1, 2) and (4, 6): the differences are 3 and 4, so the distance is √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5. For longer lists, square every difference, add them all, and take the square root. This is written ‖x − x̂‖2 and called the norm of the difference. The small 2 refers to the squaring. Other ways of measuring length exist (using a power p in place of 2), and the Wasserstein metric built with them is written Wp. For example, with p = 1 you simply add the absolute differences, so the distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6) would be 3 + 4 = 7 in place of 5.

Add the work over all cells of a plan. Since the cells are probabilities, this sum is an average, an expectation over the plan:

average work of a plan = ∫ γ(x, x̂) · ‖x − x̂‖ dx dx̂ = 𝔼(x, x̂) ~ γ[ ‖x − x̂‖ ]

For our three plans:

PlanCalculation (amount × distance, added up)Work
A: each village serves its nearest town0.5 × |0 − 1| + 0.5 × |10 − 11| = 0.5 + 0.51
B: each village serves the far town0.5 × |0 − 11| + 0.5 × |10 − 1| = 5.5 + 4.510
C: everyone ships half to each0.25 × 1 + 0.25 × 11 + 0.25 × 9 + 0.25 × 15.5

All three plans do the same job. They differ in effort.

19.4 The Wasserstein metric

Among all valid plans, take the one with the least work. That least work is the Wasserstein metric:

Wasserstein metric

W( px ‖ px̂ ) = minγ ∈ Π(x, x̂) 𝔼(x, x̂) ~ γ[ ‖x − x̂‖ ]

For the wheat, plan A is the best possible, so W = 1. That agrees with common sense: the "needed" picture is the "available" picture shifted by 1 km.

Two properties make it just what Chapter 18 asked for:

  • The closer px and px̂ are, the smaller W is. Identical distributions need no movement at all, so W = 0.
  • It does not saturate when the supports do not align, unlike an f-divergence. Go back to the point example of Chapter 18: all real mass at 0, all fake mass at θ. The only plan is to move mass 1 over a distance |θ|, so W = |θ|. That is the "true gap" row of that table, the sloping green line. At θ = 10 it says 10. At 0.01 it says 0.01. The generator always knows which way is downhill.

19.5 How do we minimise it?

The setup is as before: a generator gθ with outputs x̂ ~ pθ, and now

θ* = argminθ W( px ‖ pθ )

But we face the old difficulty of Chapter 9 again. The definition needs a search over every possible transport plan between two distributions we do not know, in a space of lakhs of dimensions. Hopeless as it stands.

Last time the rescue was the conjugate trick, which turned the divergence into a "max over a function T" of sample averages. A similar rescue exists here. The lecturer explains that every minimisation problem has a partner maximisation problem, called its dual. For the Wasserstein metric, the dual is a known result:

Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality

W( px ‖ pθ ) = max‖Tw‖L ≤ 1 [ 𝔼x ~ px[ Tw(x) ] − 𝔼x̂ ~ pθ[ Tw(x̂) ] ]

Read it: "find the function Tw that makes (its average over real samples) minus (its average over generated samples) as large as possible, and that largest value is the Wasserstein metric." Both terms are expectations, so, as we know well by now, both can be estimated by sample averages.

The only new thing is the condition written under the max: ‖Tw‖L ≤ 1. It says Tw must be 1-Lipschitz.

Detour: what is a 1-Lipschitz function?

A function is 1-Lipschitz (named after the mathematician Lipschitz) if it never changes faster than its input does. Take any two inputs. The change in the output is at most the change in the input:

‖ Tw(x1) − Tw(x2) ‖‖ x1 − x2 ‖ ≤ 1

In everyday terms: the graph is never steeper than a slope of 1, uphill or downhill.

FunctionTest with x1 = 2, x2 = 5Ratio1-Lipschitz?
T(x) = 0.5x|1 − 2.5| ÷ |2 − 5| = 1.5 ÷ 30.5Yes
T(x) = −x|−2 + 5| ÷ 3 = 3 ÷ 31Yes (just)
T(x) = 3x|6 − 15| ÷ 3 = 9 ÷ 33No

Why is the condition needed? Take the point example with real mass at 0 and fake mass at 2, where W = 2. With T(x) = −x, the bracket is T(0) − T(2) = 0 − (−2) = 2. Correct. But with T(x) = −100x the bracket would be 200, and with steeper functions it grows without limit. With no restriction, the "max" would be infinity and would mean nothing. The slope limit ties the difference in scores to the actual distance between the points.

Check the wheat example too, with T(x) = −x. Average over px: 0.5 × 0 + 0.5 × (−10) = −5. Average over px̂: 0.5 × (−1) + 0.5 × (−11) = −6. Difference: −5 − (−6) = 1. Exactly the least work we found from the tables. The two definitions agree.

19.6 The W-GAN

Put the dual form into the generator's goal:

θ*, w* = argminθ max‖Tw‖L ≤ 1 [ 𝔼x ~ px[ Tw(x) ] − 𝔼x̂ ~ pθ[ Tw(x̂) ] ]

A min over θ, a max over w, two expectations. The lecturer observes that this is very similar to a GAN, and so this method of minimising the Wasserstein metric is called the W-GAN (Wasserstein GAN). Compare it with the general form from Chapter 11, 𝔼px[T] − 𝔼pθ[f*(T)]: the W-GAN simply has no f* in the second term.

Ordinary ("naive") GANW-GAN
What is minimisedA JS-like f-divergenceThe Wasserstein metric
Second networkDiscriminator Dw, ends in a sigmoidCritic Tw, no sigmoid
Its outputA probability in [0, 1]Any real number, a score
Objective𝔼 log D(x) + 𝔼 log(1 − D(x̂))𝔼 T(x) − 𝔼 T(x̂)
Extra requirementNoneTw must be 1-Lipschitz
When supports do not alignSaturatesDoes not saturate

Example. A critic gives three real images the scores 2.0, 1.5 and 2.5 (average 2.0), and three generated images the scores −1.0, 0 and −0.5 (average −0.5). The objective is 2.0 − (−0.5) = 2.5. The critic tries to widen this gap. The generator tries to close it, by producing images that the critic scores as highly as real ones. If the generator succeeds completely, both averages are equal and the objective is 0.

In the W-GAN literature the second network is called the critic, not the discriminator, because it no longer answers "real or fake?". It gives a score, and the gap between the average score of real samples and of generated samples estimates how far apart the two distributions are.

19.7 Keeping the critic 1-Lipschitz

How do you force a neural network to be 1-Lipschitz? The lecturer says this is an area of research in itself. One practical way: normalise the weights of Tw so that ‖w‖2 = 1 after each gradient step.

"Normalise" means rescale a list of numbers so that its length (norm) becomes exactly 1. Example: weights (3, 4) have norm √(9 + 16) = 5. Divide each by 5 to get (0.6, 0.8), whose norm is √(0.36 + 0.64) = 1. The direction is kept and only the size is pulled back. For a single linear critic, a weight vector of length 1 gives the required slope limit. For a network with several layers, normalizing one list of weights alone does not guarantee it. The largest stretch of each layer matters.

So training a W-GAN is almost identical to Chapter 14:

  1. Critic turn (generator frozen): take a real batch and a generated batch, compute the average of Tw(x) minus the average of Tw(x̂), take one gradient ascent step on w, then re-normalise the weights.
  2. Generator turn (critic frozen): generate a batch and take one gradient descent step on θ. As before, only the second term involves θ.

Conclusion from the lecture

Training a W-GAN is more stable than training a naive GAN.

Try it

1. Mass 1 sits at position 2 and must all go to position 7. What is W?
2. A fourth plan for the wheat: from 0 send 0.4 to town 1 and 0.1 to town 11. From 10 send 0.1 to town 1 and 0.4 to town 11. Is it valid? What is its work?
3. Is T(x) = 2x 1-Lipschitz? Test with x1 = 1, x2 = 4.
4. Normalise the weights (6, 8) to norm 1.
5. Why is the second network of a W-GAN called a critic and not a discriminator?

Show answer

1. 1 × |2 − 7| = 5.   2. Rows: 0.5 and 0.5. Columns: 0.5 and 0.5. Valid. Work = 0.4 × 1 + 0.1 × 11 + 0.1 × 9 + 0.4 × 1 = 2.8. More than plan A's 1.   3. |2 − 8| ÷ |1 − 4| = 6 ÷ 3 = 2. No.   4. Norm is 10, so (0.6, 0.8).   5. It outputs an unrestricted score, not a probability of being real.

Chapter 19 recap

  • A transport plan is a joint distribution whose margins are px and px̂. Its work is 𝔼 ‖x − x̂‖.
  • The Wasserstein metric is the least work over all plans. It measures how far, so it does not saturate.
  • Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality: W = max over 1-Lipschitz Tw of [ 𝔼px Tw(x) − 𝔼pθ Tw(x̂) ].
  • W-GAN: min over θ, max over a critic kept 1-Lipschitz by normalising its weights after each step. Training is more stable.

20.title: Running a GAN backwards
body:
A GAN turns a code into a picture. Can we go the other way, from a picture to its code?

The problem

A trained generator gθ* is a function from the noise space to the data space, written Z → X. Give it a z and it draws a picture.

Now someone hands you a real photograph xi and asks: which z would make the generator draw this? In symbols, find zi such that gθ*(zi) = xi. This is called inversion of the GAN.

You have met inverses before. If y = 2x + 3 takes x to y, the inverse x = (y − 3) ÷ 2 takes y back to x. For a line this is easy. For a neural network with crores of knobs there is no such formula, and a plain GAN gives no way to go backwards.

A word you will see often: the noise vector z is also called the latent vector, and its space the latent space. "Latent" means hidden: z is the hidden code behind an image.

20.1 Why would anyone want this?

The lecturer lists two uses among many.

(i) Feature extraction. If the GAN is well trained, it has implicitly learned the distribution of the data. So the z behind an image is a compact description of that image: remember k ≪ d, so perhaps 100 numbers in place of 4,80,000. Given a dataset, we can invert every image and use the resulting vectors as features, short summaries that are handy for other tasks such as classification.

(ii) Data manipulation, or editing. A GAN draws new pictures, but how do you edit a picture you already have? In three steps:

1.   get zi such that xi = gθ*(zi) invert the image
2.   zedit = fedit(zi) change the code
3.   xedit = gθ*(zedit) draw the edited image

Here fedit can be any function applied to the code, for instance adding something to it or moving it along some path. For example, if the inverted code is zi = (1.0, 2.0, 0.0) and the edit is "add (0, 0, 0.5)", then zedit = (1.0, 2.0, 0.5). Editing the short code is far easier than editing lakhs of pixels by hand, and the generator makes sure the result still looks like a real image.

So the question, in the lecturer's words: how do we modify a GAN so that inversion is possible? Two answers follow.

20.2 Answer 1: the Bi-directional GAN (BiGAN)

A plain ("naive") GAN has two functions:

gθ(z) : Z → X     and     Dw(x) : X → [0, 1]

A BiGAN adds a third network, called the encoder or invertor, which goes in the opposite direction to the generator:

Eφ : X → Z

Its knobs are called φ (the Greek letter phi). It takes an image x and outputs a code ẑ = Eφ(x). Hence the name: generation in one direction, inversion in the other.

The clever part is what the discriminator looks at. In a naive GAN it classifies between x and gθ(z): single images. In a BiGAN it classifies between pairs (the lecture calls them data tuples. A tuple is simply an ordered group of things, here a pair), each made of an image and a code:

PairHow it is madeWhich part is "real"?
( x, Eφ(x) )Take a real image x ~ px. The encoder produces its codeThe image is real. The code is made by the encoder
( gθ(z), z )Take a noise vector z ~ N(0, I). The generator produces its imageThe code is real noise. The image is made by the generator

The objective is the GAN objective written for pairs. The generator and the encoder are on the same team, both trying to fool the discriminator:

minθ, φ maxw  𝔼x ~ px[ log Dw( x, Eφ(x) ) ] + 𝔼z ~ pz[ log( 1 − Dw( gθ(z), z ) ) ]

This is the loss the lecture names LBiGAN(θ, w, φ), with pz = N(0, I). It is the same shape as JGAN, with the encoder's pairs in the place of "real" and the generator's pairs in the place of "fake".

Why does this make the encoder an inverse of the generator? The lecture states that it can be shown that the optimum of LBiGAN is reached when the two kinds of pairs have the same joint distribution:

pẑx = pzx̂

Here pẑx is the joint distribution of pairs made the encoder's way (pick a real image, then encode it), and pzx̂ is the joint distribution of pairs made the generator's way (pick a code, then generate from it). Think about what the discriminator can catch. If the images in the generator's pairs do not look real, it catches that. If the codes in the encoder's pairs do not look like proper noise, it catches that. And if an image and a code are each fine but do not belong together, it catches that too. The only way to leave it helpless is for the encoder to hand each image the very code from which the generator would draw that image. That is inversion.

A toy example. Imagine a world with only two codes, 0 and 1, and only two images, A and B. The trained generator draws A from code 0 and B from code 1. So the generator's pairs are (A, 0) and (B, 1).

EncoderWhat it doesIts pairsSame as the generator's pairs?
Good encoderA → 0,   B → 1(A, 0) and (B, 1)Yes. The discriminator has nothing to catch
Bad encoderA → 1,   B → 0(A, 1) and (B, 0)No. Every image is real and every code is a valid code, but the pairings are wrong, and the discriminator learns to spot them

Only the good encoder survives, and the good encoder is exactly the inverse of the generator: it sends A back to 0 and B back to 1.

After training a BiGAN

gθ*(z) is used for generation, and Eφ*(x) is used for inversion.

20.3 Answer 2: inversion by latent regression

The second method is simpler. It also has an encoder (nothing can be done without one, says the lecturer), but it does not ask the discriminator to judge pairs. The discriminator works exactly as in a naive GAN, telling x from x̂.

The idea rests on one observation. For every generated image, we already know the right answer. We ourselves chose the z that produced it. So generated images form a free set of solved examples: image x̂, and its true code z. We can train the encoder directly on them: show it x̂, let it guess ẑ = Eφ(x̂), and penalise the gap between the guess and the truth.

Predicting numbers from an input is called regression (the kind of problem where the answer is a quantity, not a class). Here we regress the latent vector. Hence latent regression. The gap is measured by the squared distance ‖z − ẑ‖22: square each difference and add. For z = (1, 2) and ẑ = (0.5, 2.5) it is 0.5² + 0.5² = 0.5.

This penalty is simply added to the usual GAN objective:

L(θ, w, φ) = [ 𝔼x ~ px log Dw(x) + 𝔼x̂ ~ pθ log( 1 − Dw(x̂) ) ] + λ 𝔼x̂ ~ pθ[ ‖ z − Eφ(x̂) ‖22 ]

The number λ (the Greek letter lambda) is a hyperparameter. That is the name for a setting chosen by the human designer, not learned by training. Step sizes and batch sizes are hyperparameters too. Here λ decides how much weight the code-matching penalty gets compared with the GAN part. For example, if the GAN part is −0.9, the penalty is 0.5 and λ = 10, then the total is −0.9 + 10 × 0.5 = 4.1. The loss now involves three sets of knobs: the generator's θ, the discriminator's w and the encoder's (regressor's) φ.

BiGANLatent regression
Extra networkEncoder EφEncoder Eφ
Discriminator sees(image, code) pairsSingle images, as in a naive GAN
How the encoder learnsBy helping to fool the discriminator, which matches two joint distributionsBy directly predicting the known z of generated images
Extra loss termNone. The loss itself is changedλ 𝔼 ‖z − Eφ(x̂)‖²

Try it

1. A GAN uses k = 100 and images with d = 4,80,000. After inversion, how many numbers describe each image?
2. Put the three editing steps in order: generate from the edited code, invert the image, change the code.
3. In a BiGAN, which two networks are on the same side against the discriminator?
4. z = (2, 0, 1) and the encoder outputs ẑ = (1, 0, 3). What is ‖z − ẑ‖²?
5. Why can latent regression train the encoder without anyone labelling anything?

Show answer

1. 100.   2. Invert the image, change the code, generate from the edited code.   3. The generator and the encoder.   4. 1² + 0² + 2² = 5.   5. Because for every generated image the true code is already known. We picked it ourselves.

Chapter 20 recap

  • Inversion: given x, find z with gθ*(z) = x. Useful for feature extraction and for editing.
  • BiGAN: add an encoder Eφ : X → Z, and let the discriminator judge pairs (x, Eφ(x)) against (gθ(z), z). The optimum is at pẑx = pzx̂.
  • Latent regression: keep the naive GAN and add λ 𝔼 ‖z − Eφ(x̂)‖², so the encoder learns to recover the code of generated images.

21.title: The adversarial idea beyond generation
body:
The tug of war between two networks is useful even when nobody wants to generate anything. Here it repairs a classifier.

The problem

You train a classifier on thousands of labelled photographs: dog, elephant, guitar, house. It does very well on new photographs. Then somebody shows it pencil sketches of the same things, and it fails badly.

A child has no such trouble. A sketched elephant is plainly an elephant. But for the network, sketches follow a different distribution from photos, and it was only ever shown photos. The lecturer illustrates this with a standard dataset that has four styles of the same object classes: photo, art painting, cartoon and sketch.

21.1 Naming the situation

TermMeaningIn the example
Source data DSLabelled pairs {(xi, yi)}, i = 1 to n, drawn iid from a distribution pSPhotos, with labels
Target data DTSamples {x̂j}, j = 1 to m, drawn iid from a different distribution pTSketches, with no labels
Domain shiftpS ≠ pTPhotos and sketches look different
The taskClassification: estimate pS(y | x)"Given this image, which object is it?"

(In this chapter the hat on x̂ marks a target sample. Nothing is being generated.) Classifiers (or regressors, which predict a quantity) trained on DS will fail on DT, because at test time the data comes from a distribution different from the one used in training.

The setting we study is Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA). "Supervised" learning means learning from labelled examples. "Unsupervised" here refers to the target side: we have target images but no labels for them.

Objective of UDA

Given DS (labelled) and DT (unlabelled), learn features and a classifier that perform well on both pS and pT.

21.2 The idea: features that hide the domain

Split the classifier into two parts:

  • a feature extractor φ : X → F, a network that turns an image into a list of features. A photo gives source features fs = φ(x). A sketch gives target features ft = φ(x̂). (The lecture uses the letter φ again here. It is a new network, not the encoder of Chapter 20.)
  • a classifier head hψ (ψ is the Greek letter psi) that takes features and predicts the label.

Suppose we could make the feature extractor so clever that the features of photos and the features of sketches follow the same distribution. Then the classifier head, which sees only features, would not be able to tell that a sketch is a sketch. Whatever it learned from photo features would apply to sketch features too.

So we need to make two distributions match: pfs (of source features) and pft (of target features). And making two distributions match, using only samples from each, is precisely what a GAN does. That is the insight.

21.3 Domain adversarial networks

Part 1: the adversarial game. A discriminator Dw takes a feature vector and outputs a number in [0, 1]: did this come from a photo or from a sketch? It tries to tell them apart. The feature extractor tries to make that impossible.

φ*, w* = argminφ maxw  𝔼pfs[ log Dw(fs) ] + 𝔼pft[ log( 1 − Dw(ft) ) ]

It is the GAN objective once more, with source features playing "real" and target features playing "fake". The feature extractor φ sits where the generator used to be. This part is, in the lecture's words, a GAN that matches pfs = pft.

Example. Early in training, the discriminator gives photo features a score of 0.9 and sketch features 0.1: it tells them apart easily, and the objective is log 0.9 + log(1 − 0.1) = −0.21. After training, it gives 0.5 to both, and the objective is log 0.5 + log 0.5 = −1.386. The features no longer reveal which domain an image came from.

Part 2: the classification job. Matching features is useless if the features say nothing about the object. Features that are all zeros would fool the discriminator perfectly and classify nothing. So, at the same time, the classifier head and the feature extractor are trained on the labelled source data to predict the labels well:

φ*, ψ* = argminψ, φ BCE( y, hψ(fs) )

Detour: BCE, the usual penalty for classifiers

BCE stands for binary cross-entropy. It is the standard measure of how wrong a classifier's answer is, for a yes/no label. If the true label is y (1 or 0) and the classifier says "probability ŷ that it is 1":

BCE = −[ y log ŷ + (1 − y) log(1 − ŷ) ]
True yClassifier says ŷWorkingBCE
10.9−log 0.90.105
10.1−log 0.12.303
00.2−log(1 − 0.2) = −log 0.80.223

Confident and right gives a small penalty. Confident and wrong gives a large one. You have seen this before in disguise: it is the negative of the log-likelihood of Chapter 15. So minimising BCE is the same as maximising the log-likelihood, and the GAN discriminator's objective is really a BCE with the sign flipped.

So the feature extractor φ has two objectives at once:

  1. the adversarial objective: make photo features and sketch features indistinguishable, and
  2. the classification objective: keep the features useful for telling objects apart.

21.4 Using it

At inference time, the lecture says, the same classifier hψ* can be used on both source and target data, as long as it is given the features as input. For a test sketch x̂test ~ pT:

fttest = φ*( x̂test ) extract features
ŷtest = hψ*( fttest ) classify them

Since φ has ensured that pfs = pft, the classifier hψ* works the same way whatever the domain. Notice that the discriminator, as in an ordinary GAN, is needed only during training.

Common confusion: "this network generates sketches"

Nothing is generated here. There is no noise z and no generator. What is borrowed from GANs is only the adversarial principle: a discriminator trying to tell two sets of samples apart, and another network adjusting until it cannot. The lesson of this chapter is that "adversarial learning" is a general tool for making two distributions match.

Try it

1. A model trained on daytime road photos is used at night and fails. What are the source and target? What is this problem called?
2. In UDA, which dataset has labels?
3. A lazy feature extractor outputs the same feature vector for every image. Which objective is it satisfying, and which is it failing?
4. Compute the BCE when y = 0 and ŷ = 0.9.

Show answer

1. Source: daytime photos. Target: night photos. Domain shift.   2. Only the source.   3. It satisfies the adversarial objective (no discriminator can tell the domains apart) and fails the classification objective (identical features cannot separate classes).   4. −log(1 − 0.9) = −log 0.1 = 2.303. Confident and wrong.

Chapter 21 recap

  • Domain shift: training data and test data come from different distributions, pS ≠ pT.
  • UDA: labelled source, unlabelled target, and we want good performance on both.
  • Domain adversarial network: a feature extractor φ, a classifier hψ and a discriminator Dw.
  • φ plays a GAN-style game against Dw to make pfs = pft, and also minimises the BCE for classification with hψ.

22.title: Giving a generator its marks
body:
We have trained a generator. Is it any good? This last chapter shows the most popular way to answer with a number.

The problem

A classifier is easy to grade: count how many test examples it labels correctly. A generator has no "correct answer" to compare with. Each output is new. You could look at a few images and say "these seem nice", but that is slow, differs from person to person, and tells you nothing about variety. A generator that draws the same one beautiful cat every time would pass.

The lecturer's question: how do we validate a trained generative model? He notes there are several metrics, and presents one.

22.1 The setup

SetWhat it is
Dtrue = {x1, …, xn} ~ iid pxThe real data, the same input data the model was trained on
Dgen = {x̂1, …, x̂n} ~ iid pθ*Generated data: outputs of the trained generator

Goal: compare Dtrue and Dgen as whole collections. We are back to our oldest question, how far apart two distributions are, this time for marking, not for training. A popular metric for this is the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID). In the lecture's words, FID is the Wasserstein metric between Dtrue and Dgen. It is computed in five steps.

22.2 The five steps of FID

Step (i). Take a pretrained Inception network. "Inception" is the name of a well-known deep CNN. It was trained on ImageNet, a very large collection of labelled photographs, to recognise objects. Pretrained means the training is already done by someone else: we take the network with its knobs fixed and only use it. It is written Iψ*(x).

Step (ii). Pass both sets through it and collect features. We do not want its final answer ("this is a cat"). We stop partway, at the output of some layer number l, and take the numbers found there. That list of numbers is a feature vector for the image. Which layer to use is a hyperparameter (a choice made by the designer). The lecturer gives the 64th layer as an example.

Why features and not raw pixels? Two photos of the same cat, one shifted slightly to the left, differ in almost every pixel, but a network trained to recognise objects gives them nearly the same features. Features describe what is in the picture. That is the level at which we want to compare.

We now have two sets of feature vectors:

D̂true = { z1true, …, zntrue }     and     D̂gen = { z1gen, …, zngen }

where each zi is the output of the l-th layer for image number i. (This z is a feature vector. It has nothing to do with the generator's noise. The small raised i is a counter, not a power.)

Step (iii). Compute the mean and the covariance of each set.

Detour: mean vector, covariance, matrix and trace, with one small example

Suppose we have just 4 images, and each image has just 2 features, a and b:

ImageFeature aFeature b
112
232
334
454

Mean vector. Average each feature separately. For a: (1 + 3 + 3 + 5) ÷ 4 = 3. For b: (2 + 2 + 4 + 4) ÷ 4 = 3. The mean vector, written μ (the Greek letter mu), is (3, 3). In symbols:

μtrue = 1n Σi=1n zitrue

Variance of each feature. As in Chapter 3: the average squared distance from the mean.

Imagea − 3b − 3(a − 3)²(b − 3)²(a − 3) × (b − 3)
1−2−1412
20−1010
301010
421412
Average8 ÷ 4 = 24 ÷ 4 = 14 ÷ 4 = 1

So the variance of a is 2 and the variance of b is 1.

Covariance. The last column is new. It multiplies the two distances together and averages them. This number, 1, is the covariance of a and b. It tells us whether the two features rise and fall together. Here it is positive: images with a larger a tend to have a larger b too. (Think of height and weight: taller students tend to be heavier.) If one tended to fall when the other rose, the covariance would be negative. If they had nothing to do with each other, it would be about 0.

Matrix. A matrix is simply a rectangular table of numbers. We collect the variances and covariances into a square one, called the covariance matrix and written Σ (capital sigma, the same letter as the sum sign, used here as a name):

Σab
a21
b11

The entries on the diagonal (top-left to bottom-right, shown in bold) are the variances. The other entries are the covariances. With 2 features the matrix is 2 × 2. With 2,000 features it is 2,000 × 2,000, built in the same way. (The lecture's board writes the short form Σ = (1/n) Σi zi(zi)T, which is this calculation for features measured from their mean.)

Trace. The trace of a square matrix, written tr, is the sum of its diagonal entries. Here tr(Σ) = 2 + 1 = 3. It turns a whole table into one number: the total spread.

Square root of a matrix. The formula ahead contains a matrix raised to the power ½. That means "the matrix which, multiplied by itself, gives this one". For a matrix with numbers only on the diagonal it is easy: take the square root of each. A matrix with 4 and 9 on its diagonal has a square root with 2 and 3 on its diagonal. For other matrices a computer does the work.

So each set is summarised by a centre and a spread: μtrue, Σtrue and μgen, Σgen.

Step (iv). Assume both sets of features are Gaussian.

ztrue ~ N( μtrue, Σtrue )     and     zgen ~ N( μgen, Σgen )

This is an assumption, and the lecture labels it so. A bell-shaped distribution in many dimensions is completely described by its mean vector and covariance matrix, just as the one-dimensional bell curve was described by mean and variance in Chapter 3. Making this assumption is what allows the next step.

Step (v). Compute the Wasserstein metric between the two Gaussians. In general the Wasserstein metric needs a search over transport plans (Chapter 19). But between two Gaussians it is given directly by a formula, with no search at all:

FID

FID = ‖ μtrue − μgen ‖22 + tr( Σtrue + Σgen − 2 ( Σtrue Σgen )½ )

Both parts are single numbers. The first is a squared length. The second is a trace.

  • The first part compares the centres: are the generated images, on average, about the same things as the real ones?
  • The second part compares the spreads: do the generated images have the same variety as the real ones?

22.3 FID with one feature

To see what the formula does, suppose each image had just one feature. Then μ is a single number, Σ is just the variance σ², and the trace of a single number is itself. The second part becomes σt² + σg² − 2σtσg, which is the Class 9 identity for (σt − σg)². So:

FID (one feature) = ( μtrue − μgen )² + ( σtrue − σgen )²

Say the real images have feature mean 5 and standard deviation 2. Compare three generators:

GeneratorMeanStd. dev.WorkingFID
A: close in both5.51.8(5 − 5.5)² + (2 − 1.8)² = 0.25 + 0.040.29
B: off-centre, and little variety80.5(5 − 8)² + (2 − 0.5)² = 9 + 2.2511.25
C: identical statistics520 + 00

Generator B is punished twice: its images are about the wrong things (centre off by 3) and they all look alike (spread 0.5 where it should be 2). That second penalty is exactly what "looking at a few nice samples" could never catch.

With two features. If the features do not vary together (all covariances are 0), the formula simply adds the one-feature result over the features. Say the real images have means (5, 2) and standard deviations (2, 1), and a generator gives means (5.5, 2.5) and standard deviations (1.8, 1.5).

FeatureCentre partSpread partSum
First(5 − 5.5)² = 0.25(2 − 1.8)² = 0.040.29
Second(2 − 2.5)² = 0.25(1 − 1.5)² = 0.250.50
FID0.79

In the formula's language: the centre part is ‖μtrue − μgen‖² = 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5, and the trace part adds the spread terms along the diagonal, 0.04 + 0.25 = 0.29. Total 0.79.

22.4 Reading the result

Lower is better

The generative model is better if its FID is lower. A lower FID means a lower Wasserstein distance between px and pθ*.

Common confusion: FID is not accuracy

Accuracy runs from 0% to 100% and higher is better. FID is a distance: 0 is the ideal, there is no upper limit, and lower is better. It is also only meaningful for comparing models evaluated in the same way: same real data, same feature layer.

Try it

1. Real features: mean 10, standard deviation 3. Generator P: mean 9, standard deviation 3. Generator Q: mean 10, standard deviation 1. Compute the one-feature FID of each. Which is better?
2. What is the trace of a table whose diagonal entries are 4, 1 and 2?
3. Why does FID compare features from an Inception network and not raw pixels?
4. A generator memorises one real image and outputs it every time. Which part of the FID formula will be large?

Show answer

1. P: (10 − 9)² + 0 = 1. Q: 0 + (3 − 1)² = 4. P is better.   2. 4 + 1 + 2 = 7.   3. Features describe what is in the image and are not thrown off by small shifts in the pixels.   4. The second part. The generated set has almost no spread, so its covariance is far from that of the real set.

Chapter 22 recap

  • To grade a generator, compare a set of real images with a set of generated ones.
  • FID: pass both through a pretrained Inception network, take features from a chosen layer, compute mean and covariance of each set, assume Gaussians, and compute the Wasserstein metric between them by formula.
  • FID = ‖μtrue − μgen‖² + tr( Σtrue + Σgen − 2(ΣtrueΣgen)½ ).
  • Lower FID = better generator.

recap.title: The whole journey on one page
body:
With this, the lectures say, the topic of adversarial learning ends. Here is everything you have learned, as one chain of ideas.

PartThe questionThe answer
1 (Ch. 1–6)What is generative modelling?Data are samples from an unknown distribution px. Build a network gθ that turns noise into samples from pθ, and choose θ to make a divergence between px and pθ small
1 (Ch. 7–10)How do we measure that divergence from samples alone?Use an f-divergence, and the conjugate trick turns it into a lower bound made of two sample averages and a helper function T
2 (Ch. 11–14)How does that become a working machine?Make T a second network. Min over θ, max over w. With a JS-like f this is the GAN, trained by alternating gradient steps
3 (Ch. 15–17)How do we understand it and use it better?It is a generator guided by a classifier. Build it with (transpose) convolutions for images. Feed in a label to control the output
4 (Ch. 18–19)Why does it get stuck, and what is the cure?Real and generated data lie on thin sheets that do not overlap, so f-divergences go flat. The Wasserstein metric measures how far, and gives the W-GAN
4 (Ch. 20–22)What else can we do?Invert a GAN (BiGAN, latent regression), match features across domains (domain adversarial networks), and grade generators (FID)

Go back for a moment to Riya and the poem in Chapter 1. She asked how a machine can make something new. You can now give the real answer: it has adjusted the knobs of a network until its outputs follow the same hidden distribution as the examples it was shown, and a fresh piece of noise then gives a fresh sample from that distribution.

What comes after this book. The course moves on from GANs to the other families listed in Chapter 1: variational auto-encoders, diffusion models, auto-regressive language models, state-space models, and alignment methods. The ideas you now own (distributions, divergences, lower bounds, expectations estimated from samples) are the foundation for all of them.

How to read this book

Read slowly, with a pencil. When you see a Try it box, stop and actually try it before opening the answer. Yellow Detour boxes teach a piece of maths you have not met in school yet. Red Common confusion boxes warn you about the mistakes almost everybody makes. Every chapter ends with a short recap, so if you get lost, jump to the recap and come back.

Where we are

Chapter 6 ended with a machine gθ that turns noise into data, and one painful question: how do we compute the divergence D( px ‖ pθ ) when we know neither px nor pθ? These four chapters answer it. The method has a long name, variational divergence minimisation, and the famous GAN is one member of this family. These are the hardest chapters in the book. Go slowly. Nothing here needs more than patience.

Where we are

Part 1 ended with this result, which uses only averages over samples:

Df( px ‖ pθ )  ≥  maxT [ 𝔼px[ T(x) ] − 𝔼pθ[ f*( T(x) ) ] ]

From here on the lectures write max where they earlier wrote sup. As agreed in Chapter 7, they mean the same thing for us. Part 2 turns this formula into a working machine.

Where we are

Parts 1 and 2 reached the GAN by a long road: f-divergence, lower bound, a helper function, a special choice of f. The result was

θ*, w* = argminθ maxw [ 𝔼x~px log Dw(x) + 𝔼x̂~pθ log( 1 − Dw(x̂) ) ]

Part 3 is lighter on maths. It gives a second, shorter road to the same formula, and then two improvements that make GANs useful in practice.

Where we are

We can build a GAN, design it for images, and steer it with labels. The lecturer now turns to two things: improvements that make adversarial training more stable, and a few applications of adversarial learning other than generating data.
